chart_gl.title: Accounts 1 — The Chart of Accounts & the General Ledger
chart_gl.desc: The foundation of the accounts layer: the General Ledger written by documents, the debit-credit grammar with the direction table, the Chart of Accounts designed from the reading list with the account-versus-dimension rule, the account types that wire the machinery, the posting map document by document, reading the GL and the trial balance anomaly scan, and the control-to-party tie with its monthly check — opening the HealthTrade case.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Books that write themselves
lessons.html:
This track certifies you on the accounts layer of ZhiftERP: the General Ledger, the Chart of Accounts, journals, banking, receivables and payables, tax, dimensions, the period close, and the settings that govern all of it. This module covers the foundation: how the ledger works, how the chart is designed, and how to read both.

The General Ledger. Every financial event in the business becomes a dated entry in the General Ledger (GL): an account, a debit or credit, an amount, and the document that caused it. Entries are added and never edited — corrections are new entries posted beside the old ones (module 2 covers the rules). The GL is the money twin of the stock ledger: both are permanent records written by documents, and some documents write both at once — a delivery moves stock and posts the cost of goods sold in the same act.

The central idea: the books are written by documents. In ZhiftERP, a properly used trading system produces its own books:

• A sales invoice posts the revenue, the VAT, and the customer's debt.
• A purchase receipt posts the stock value and the accrual for the unbilled goods.
• A payment entry posts the bank movement and clears the debt.

Nobody journalises any of this — each document carries its accounting inside it. The accounting work therefore changes shape: instead of writing entries all day, you govern the machine — the chart it posts into (this module), the few manual entries it genuinely needs (module 2), the reconciliations that prove it (module 3), and the statements it produces (module 7). A business that hand-journalises its sales while the trading modules sit idle has declined the system's whole premise; recognising that situation, and knowing how to fix it, is part of this certification.

What this module teaches. Chapter 2: debits and credits — the two-word grammar every GL entry speaks. Chapters 3-4: the Chart of Accounts — its tree structure, its design rules, and the account types that wire accounts into the machinery. Chapter 5: the posting map — exactly which entries each document writes; the reference card for the whole track. Chapter 6: reading the GL and the trial balance. Chapter 7: control accounts and party ledgers — the tie between a total and its details. Chapter 8: the case study — HealthTrade, the pharmaceutical distributor this track follows, designing its chart in one afternoon. Chapter 9: review and the module's law.

One orientation before starting. The chart and the ledger are read far more often than they are written. Every design decision in this module is judged by one question: does it make the books easier to read?

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Debits and credits
lessons.html:
Every GL entry uses two words — debit and credit. Learn the grammar once in this chapter and every entry in the system becomes readable.

The equation. The books describe one reality twice: Assets = Liabilities + Equity — what the business has equals who has claims on it — with income and expenses as equity's running story. Every event touches at least two accounts, and every entry's debits equal its credits: money that came from somewhere went somewhere, and the entry records both ends.

The direction table. Memorise this; it is the whole grammar:

• Assets (bank, debtors, stock, equipment) — debit to increase, credit to decrease.
• Expenses (rent, salaries, COGS) — debit to increase. Expenses move like assets, which is the table's one merciful simplification.
• Liabilities (creditors, VAT payable, loans) — credit to increase, debit to decrease.
• Income (sales, other income) — credit to increase.
• Equity (capital, retained earnings) — credit to increase.

The mnemonic: DEAD — Debits increase Expenses, Assets, Drawings; everything else grows by credit.

Three familiar documents, read in the grammar.

1. A sales invoice for ₦107,500 (₦100,000 + VAT): DEBIT Debtors ₦107,500 (an asset grew — the customer owes you), CREDIT Sales ₦100,000 (income grew), CREDIT VAT Payable ₦7,500 (a liability grew — tax money held in custody for FIRS). Debits ₦107,500 = credits ₦107,500.
2. The customer's payment: DEBIT Bank ₦107,500 (asset up), CREDIT Debtors ₦107,500 (asset down — the claim became cash).
3. A purchase receipt of stock at ₦940,000: DEBIT Stock ₦940,000 (asset up), CREDIT Stock Received But Not Billed ₦940,000 (a liability — you hold goods you have not yet been invoiced for; Chapter 5 completes this thread).

What the grammar lets you read.

• The balance side. Each account normally carries one side. Debtors carries a debit balance; a credit balance on a customer means you owe them — usually an unallocated advance. The wrong-side balance is always a story worth opening.
• The growth read. Credits growing Sales is trade; debits growing Sales is returns and reversals — worth a look when large.
• The other side. Every entry has a counterparty account. When an entry looks wrong, read its other side — the expense that was credited, the bank that was debited twice — and the mistake usually names itself.

Practical rule: when any balance or entry confuses you, say it out loud in the grammar — which account, which side, grew by what. Most confusion does not survive the sentence.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The Chart of Accounts: designing the tree
lessons.html:
Every account lives in the Chart of Accounts, which is a tree: group nodes for organising and reading, and ledger accounts — the leaves — for posting. Every GL entry names a leaf; posting to a group fails by design. Money exists in accounts; groups exist so accounts can be read together.

The fixed roots. Four (or five) root types anchor everything: Assets, Liabilities, Equity, Income, Expenses — the equation's own families. Beneath them, groups organise for reading (Current Assets → Bank Accounts → the individual banks; Indirect Expenses → Administrative → the specific lines), and the leaves take the postings.

Design from the reading, not the listing. The standard chart the system ships is a competent skeleton. The design work is tailoring it to how this business asks questions:

1. Write down the owner's monthly questions first — what did we make, what did it cost, where did the money go. These define the P&L groups.
2. Add the statement's needs and the audit's. These define the balance-sheet shape.
3. Apply the granularity test to every proposed account: an account earns its existence when someone will read its line separately. Three bank accounts are three leaves because three reconciliations will happen. Office Expenses split into eleven micro-accounts nobody reads separately is sprawl.

Accounts versus dimensions. A distinction nobody reads as its own account line belongs to a dimension, not an account. The chart answers what kind of money; dimensions (module 6) answer whose and where — the branch, the service line. Mixing them up is how charts explode into per-branch copies of every expense line. Rule: one chart, one language; the branches become a lens on it, not copies of it.

Naming, numbering, and depth.

• Names that read plainly in every report — the accountant's vocabulary, not the software's.
• Numbering where the business's reporting tradition uses it: consistent, gapped for insertion, never re-used.
• Shape: shallow. Two to three levels below root serves almost every trading business; a five-level chart is bureaucracy nobody navigates.

Change discipline. Charts live for decades:

• Renaming a leaf is cheap — the history follows the account.
• Restructuring — re-parenting groups, merging accounts — changes how history reads, so it is planned, done at a period boundary, and documented.
• Creation rights are narrow. New accounts are proposed against the reading test, not created per whim. Chapter 9's sprawl pattern is what happens otherwise.

Practical rule: the finished chart should pass a one-line test — every account has a one-sentence explanation of who reads it and why. An account that fails the test should not exist.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Account types: the wiring
lessons.html:
Two leaves can sit side by side in the tree and behave completely differently, because beneath the position sits the account type — and the type is what wires an account into the system's machinery. Names are for humans; types are for the machine.

The types and what each enables.

• Bank and Cash — join the payment machinery: payment modes point at them, and — decisively — Bank-type accounts join the bank reconciliation (module 3). A real-world bank account modelled as any other type is invisible to the reconciliation that proves it.
• Receivable and Payable — the control accounts: entries here require a party (the customer or supplier). This is what makes per-party ledgers possible — the control account is the total, the party is the detail (Chapter 7). An invoice posted to a non-Receivable account has left the machinery that ages, allocates and produces statements.
• Stock — the accounts the perpetual-inventory machinery writes: stock-in-hand, the received-not-billed accrual, the adjustment homes. Manual journals against Stock-type accounts are fenced, because the stock ledger and the GL must stay in agreement (module 2, Chapter 6).
• Tax — the VAT and WHT accounts the tax templates post to: typed so the tax machinery and its reports can find them, and reconciled monthly against their registers.
• Fixed Asset, Depreciation, Accumulated Depreciation — the asset machinery's accounts (module 7 covers fixed assets).
• Round-off, exchange gain/loss, temporary opening — the system's designated homes for its own arithmetic edges. Configured once, reviewed for reasonableness — a steadily growing round-off account is a symptom, not rounding.

Three type rules.

1. Type at creation. Set the type correctly when the account is born. Retyping an account that has history is an event bordering on a migration — a receivable that spent a year untyped has a year of party-less entries that no toggle repairs.
2. When a posting misbehaves, suspect the type first. The invoice that will not accept a party, the bank missing from the reconciliation list — check the account's type before names, before permissions.
3. Defaults complete the wiring. The company's default accounts — debtors, creditors, stock accounts, round-off, exchange difference — must point at correctly typed leaves. A wrong default mis-posts every document that relies on it, silently, from day one. Verify the defaults during setup, and re-verify after any chart restructuring.

Practical rule: once a year, audit the types — every Bank-type account against the real bank list, every control account against its party machinery, every default against its intended leaf. Thirty minutes, and the class of errors in rule 2 stops occurring.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The posting map
lessons.html:
This chapter makes the books-write-themselves idea concrete: the posting map — exactly which GL entries each document writes. Learn it once and every GL question becomes a lookup. This is the reference card of the whole track.

Sales Invoice. DR Debtors (party: the customer) for the gross; CR Sales for the net; CR VAT Payable for the tax. Where Update Stock is on (the POS-style flow), the invoice also does the delivery's work: CR Stock, DR COGS.

Delivery Note. The stock movement's money shadow: CR Stock (value leaves at the valuation method's figure), DR COGS. No revenue posts here — delivery moves value, invoicing books revenue — which is why a period's deliveries and invoices must both be complete before its margin is true (module 7's cut-off discipline starts here).

Payment Entry (received). DR Bank (the payment mode's account), CR Debtors (party) — the claim becomes cash. Deductions ride as extra lines in the same entry: WHT withheld at source debits its receivable asset account alongside the bank line.

Purchase Receipt. DR Stock at landed valuation; CR Stock Received But Not Billed — the accrual that says we hold goods we have not yet been invoiced for. Useful diagnostic: the RNB account's balance is the open goods-received-awaiting-invoice queue, in naira. An old, large RNB balance means unbilled receipts are aging — readable straight from the GL.

Purchase Invoice. CR Creditors (party: the supplier); DR the RNB accrual (clearing it — the possession is now billed); DR Input VAT (the claimable asset). Where no receipt preceded it — a service invoice — the expense account is debited directly. WHT withheld from the supplier posts its credit to WHT Payable inside the payment entry that settles the invoice.

Stock Entries. Issues and write-offs: CR Stock, DR the expense account the entry names. Material receipts: DR Stock, CR the designated offset account. Transfers: silent in the P&L — value travels, nothing is earned or consumed.

Stock Reconciliation. The count adjustment's money face: DR/CR Stock against the adjustment account — the shrinkage figure landing in the P&L where policy directed it.

Journal Entry. Whatever its author says — which is exactly its power and its danger, and why module 2 exists.

Using the map. Three habits:

1. Verify it live at setup. Post one small real document of each kind and read its entries against the map. A mis-wired default or template is caught in an hour instead of inherited by a month of postings.
2. Diagnose backwards. A strange GL entry names its document; the map tells you what that document should have written; the difference locates the problem.
3. Explain forwards. When anyone asks why an account moved, the map turns the answer into one sentence — the account is written by these documents, and here are the period's instances.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Reading the GL and the trial balance
lessons.html:
The General Ledger report is the diagnostic read of this track: it answers how any balance got to be what it is. This chapter is the reading method.

The GL report's filters.

• By account — the account's full story between dates: opening balance, every entry, closing balance.
• By party — a customer or supplier across accounts: their whole financial relationship on one screen.
• By voucher — one document's complete footprint: the posting map, verified live.
• By cost center or dimension — module 6's lens.

Each entry shows its date, accounts, amounts, party, remarks — and its document, which is the point of the whole design.

The drill-down. Every number in the system can be walked to its paper: statement line → account balance → GL entries → the document → its attachments. Three or four clicks from any report figure to the document that caused it. Use it as the standing habit:

• The disputed figure is opened live in the meeting, not researched afterwards.
• The strange balance is walked to its entries the same day.
• The month-end query is answered with a filtered GL, not a recollection.

A business whose managers drill down argues from documents; one whose managers export to spreadsheets argues from tabs. Build the first habit — it sets in the first month or not at all.

The trial balance. The GL's summary face: every account, its period debits, credits, and closing balance. It always balances — the grammar guarantees that — so it is read not for its total but for its anomalies:

• The account that should be zero and is not. The RNB accrual aging, a suspense account with a growing balance, a round-off account trending upward.
• The balance on the wrong side. A credit-balance customer (an unallocated advance), a debit-balance VAT Payable — each one a story the grammar makes readable.
• The account nobody recognises. Chapter 9's pattern; the annual chart walk retires it.

The monthly scan. Ten minutes, once a month: run the trial balance, flag the anomalies, open each one to its entries. This scan is the accounts layer's version of cycle counting — small and rhythmic — and it is the reason the year-end close holds no surprises. Module 7 gives the close its full checklist; the scan is the everyday version.

Practical rule: never leave a wrong-side balance or an unexplained account for the close to find. The entry that explains it is four clicks away today and an archaeology project in six months.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Control accounts and the party tie
lessons.html:
One structure deserves its own chapter before module 4 builds on it: the control account and its party ledger, and the tie that keeps both trustworthy.

The structure. Debtors is one leaf in the chart — one balance, the total of every customer's claim. But every entry to it carried a party (Chapter 4's type rule), so the system maintains, in effect, a ledger per customer inside the account:

• The GL filtered by party is the customer's statement.
• The receivables report ages the parties.
• The control account's balance is, by construction, the sum of its parties' balances.

The same structure serves Creditors. The pattern: the control is the total; the parties are the detail; they agree because they are the same entries read two ways.

How the tie breaks. The agreement holds automatically — until someone posts around the machinery:

• A journal entry to Debtors without a party — a naira in the control that belongs to no customer. The total now exceeds the details, and every customer statement is silently suspect.
• A balance corrected at the control level while the party detail stands — the same divergence, reversed.
• A migration that loaded totals without party detail — the tie broken from birth.

Once diverged, reconciling a control back to its parties is archaeology. The discipline is therefore prevention:

1. Party-typed accounts take party-carrying entries only. The system enforces most of this; module 2's journal rules fence the rest.
2. The monthly tie check: the control account's balance against the party report's total, agreeing to the kobo. It joins the close checklist alongside the other standing agreements — stock ledger to stock accounts, tax registers to tax accounts. The shared principle: a total the details cannot reproduce is a total nobody should trust.

What an intact tie buys.

• The ageing reports are believed — collections and the payment run both work from them.
• Customer and supplier statements go out without fear: the statement is the party ledger, printed.
• The auditor samples parties and finds the control every time — the confirmation exercise ends early.
• The balance sheet's receivables line is a number with hundreds of defensible components, not one asserted total.

Practical rule: the subledger habits taught at the sales and purchasing desks — allocate payments to invoices, match advances, carry references — are all, from this chair, tie maintenance. When the tie check disagrees, the first suspect is always a journal (module 2, Chapter 6 explains why), and the GL's journal filter on the control accounts finds it in minutes.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's chart is born
lessons.html:
HealthTrade is the pharmaceutical distributor this track follows — three branches, an in-house accountant, and a newly implemented ZhiftERP system. This chapter is the afternoon its chart was designed, following Chapters 1-7 in order.

Step 1 — the reading list (Chapter 3). Before any account is touched, the MD's monthly questions are written down: sales and margin (eventually by branch — noted for module 6's dimensions), what running the business costs (rent, people, power, logistics — each read separately), and what the business owns and owes (banks by account, stock, debtors, creditors, the tax custodies). The accountant adds the statement's needs and the audit's. The list — fifteen questions — becomes the chart's specification.

Step 2 — tailoring the skeleton (Chapters 3-4). The standard chart is walked against the list:

• The three real banks become three Bank-type leaves under Bank Accounts — three reconciliations coming in module 3.
• Debtors and Creditors are confirmed as typed control accounts.
• The Stock family is confirmed wired to the perpetual-inventory machinery.
• The tax custodies are named plainly: VAT Payable, Input VAT, WHT Payable, WHT Receivable.
• The expense groups are shaped to the reading list — eleven micro-splits of administrative expenses collapsed to four lines someone will actually read.
• The branch question is answered the right way: not per-branch copies of every expense account, but a dimension, noted for module 6. One chart, one language; the branches become a lens.

Names in the accountant's vocabulary; numbering per their tradition; two levels below root, nowhere three.

Step 3 — the posting map verified live (Chapter 5). One small, real document of each kind is posted and its entries read against the map: a test invoice (Debtors gross, Sales net, VAT Payable — the grammar read aloud); a purchase receipt (the RNB accrual explained: this balance is your unbilled possession — watch it clear when the invoice books); a delivery's COGS line tied to the stock valuation; a payment's allocation read in the party ledger. Two defaults are corrected on the spot — the round-off account pointed at a sensible home, and one payment mode mapped to the wrong bank. The hour does exactly what Chapter 5 promised: the mis-wires are caught before a month inherits them.

Step 4 — the first reads (Chapters 6-7). The GL drill is demonstrated to the accountant: statement → account → entries → document, four clicks. The trial balance is scanned and one anomaly found immediately — a small credit balance on a customer, drilled to an unallocated advance from the go-live week, allocated the same day. The monthly rhythms are diarised: the ten-minute trial balance scan, and the control-to-party tie check. The accountant's note at the end of the afternoon: the chart answers my questions instead of the software's. That is the first chart I have ever said that about.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the first law
lessons.html:
The recurring chart-and-ledger mistakes, each with its symptom, cause and fix. Check yourself against these — they are also quiz material.

Pattern 1 — chart sprawl. Symptom: four hundred accounts for an eleven-person business; nobody can say what half are for; every report is a scroll. Cause: accounts created per whim — one per project, per branch, per mood (Chapter 3). Fix: apply the reading test in a consolidation pass — balances merged by documented entries into accounts that are actually read, unused accounts retired; creation rights narrowed; dimensions carrying the distinctions that were never account-shaped.

Pattern 2 — the suspense squatter. Symptom: a suspense or miscellaneous account with a large, aging, growing balance. Cause: the account meant for momentary parking used as a destination for everything unclassifiable (Chapters 3, 6). Fix: suspense swept to zero monthly as a close-checklist line — each item classified to its true home — and the classification gaps that fed it fixed at the source: a default, a template, or training.

Pattern 3 — the untyped leaf. Symptom: a bank missing from the reconciliation; an invoice refusing a party; receivables that cannot age. Cause: accounts created with names instead of types (Chapter 4) — the machinery is wired to types, and the leaf is invisible to it. Fix: type at creation as a rule; retyping-with-history treated as the serious event it is; the annual type audit.

Pattern 4 — the party-less posting. Symptom: the control disagreeing with its parties; customer statements missing money everyone knows exists. Cause: entries to control accounts without parties — journals posted around the machinery (Chapter 7; module 2 owns the fence). Fix: the divergence reconciled once (priced honestly as the archaeology it is), the journal rules installed, and the monthly tie check standing guard afterwards.

Pattern 5 — the account nobody can explain. Symptom: the trial balance line that draws blank looks in the meeting. Cause: the chart accumulated instead of designed (Chapter 3). Fix: the annual walk with the accountant — each unexplainable account investigated to its entries (the GL always knows), then merged, retired, or documented. The deliverable: a chart where every line has a one-sentence explanation.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can state: the direction table and DEAD; the three worked documents from Chapter 2; the reading test and the account-versus-dimension rule; the type wiring and the three type rules; the posting map document by document; the GL filters, the drill-down, and the trial balance anomaly read; the control-to-party structure, how the tie breaks, and the monthly tie check.

The first law: the books are written by documents, into a chart designed for reading. Module 2 opens the one deliberate exception — the Journal Entry — and the rules that keep it safe.

journal_entries.title: Accounts 2 — Journal Entries & the Manual Layer
journal_entries.desc: The Journal Entry as the one governed exception: what the journal bypasses, its fields and their rules, the lawful list with the document and evidence tests, accruals and prepayments worked with figures, the four correction rules, the forbidden list with what each journal breaks, and the controls — two named holders, thresholds, one page of templates, and the five-question monthly review.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The one door: the Journal Entry
lessons.html:
Module 1 described a ledger written by documents. This module covers the one deliberate exception: the Journal Entry — the document whose only job is to write the GL directly, any accounts, any amounts, whatever its author enters. It exists because real accounting genuinely needs it (Chapter 3 lists the lawful uses, and they are monthly). It is dangerous because of what it bypasses. This module teaches both halves.

What the journal bypasses. Every trading document carries machinery around its GL posting:

• The invoice maintains the party ledger, feeds the VAT register, and ages into collections.
• The receipt writes the stock ledger beside the money.
• The payment allocates against its references.

The journal carries none of that. It writes bare GL lines, and every naira it posts has skipped the systems that make totals decomposable: the party tie, the stock-to-accounts agreement, the tax registers, the invoice match queue. That is not a flaw — the journal is specialised for events that have no trading document (rent accruing, depreciation charging). But the specialisation cuts both ways: used where a document exists, the journal fixes the GL's number while breaking every detail beneath it — and the break is silent. The trial balance still balances, the statements still print, and the divergence surfaces weeks later as a tie that will not reconcile. Most books rot exactly this way — not through fraud, through convenience.

The module's rule, stated now. The journal is the exception and the document is the rule: what a document can do, a document must do. Sales are invoiced, never journalised. Purchases are billed. Stock moves by stock documents. Payments are payment entries. The journal takes what remains — the genuine list in Chapter 3, under the controls in Chapter 7.

The habit you will meet. Accountants trained on manual books often journalise everything — some systems are, in practice, a GL with ten thousand journals and no trading documents at all. The habit is not incompetence; it is fluency in the old instrument. The fix is transferring the fluency: every recurring journal examined for the document that should replace it, corrections routed through Chapter 5's rules, and the monthly journal count watched as a health figure — a trading business's lawful journal traffic is small, so a large or growing count is itself a finding.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the journal's fields and the rules attached to each. Chapter 3: the lawful list. Chapter 4: accruals and prepayments, worked with figures. Chapter 5: the correction rules. Chapter 6: the forbidden list — journals that break machinery. Chapter 7: who may journal, and the monthly review. Chapter 8: HealthTrade's manual layer. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The journal entry, field by field
lessons.html:
The controls in this module are enforced in the journal's own fields. This chapter covers each field and its rule.

The rows. Each row carries an account, a debit or credit amount, and the extras the account's type demands:

• Party — required where the account is a Receivable or Payable control. A journal can lawfully touch Debtors, but only carrying the customer it concerns (and Chapter 6 narrows even that).
• Cost center / dimension — where P&L accounts carry their address (module 6). A journal that charges an expense must still say whose expense.
• References — where a row settles against existing entries.

The balance rule. Total debits must equal total credits or the entry will not save. A journal that seems to need to be one-sided is a misdiagnosis: the other side exists, and the author has not found it yet. Parking the difference in suspense is not the answer — Chapter 9 covers where that habit leads.

Posting date. When the entry speaks. Rules:

• Honest dates always — the accrual for March is dated in March.
• Closed periods are respected — the period-close settings block postings into finalised months (module 8 covers the settings).
• Accrual reversals date forward — the estimate posted at month-end reverses on the 1st of the next month (Chapter 4's pattern).

Entry type. The classification field: Journal Entry, Bank Entry, Cash Entry, Contra Entry (bank-to-bank and cash-to-bank movements — module 3 uses these), Credit Note and Debit Note journals, Depreciation Entry, and others. The type does two jobs: some light machinery work (Contra entries join the bank reconciliation's world), and heavy review work — the monthly journal review reads by type, and a mis-typed entry hides from its reviewer. Type entries correctly.

Reference number and date. The external anchor: the bank advice, the payroll summary, the agreement clause — the paper this journal answers to. Fill it whenever such paper exists.

Remarks. The story field, and the most strictly enforced rule in this module: every journal narrates itself — what happened, why this entry, what evidence supports it. Trading documents are their own explanation; a journal's explanation lives only here. A journal with empty remarks is unusable six months later — nobody, including its author, can say why it exists, and any review (internal or audit) treats it accordingly. The remarks rule has no exceptions. Recurring templates (Chapter 7) carry their stories pre-written, so the rule costs nothing where the traffic is routine.

Summary. Rows balanced, parties on control accounts, dimensions on P&L lines, honest dates, correct types, external references attached, and a story in the remarks — every time.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The lawful list
lessons.html:
The discipline of Chapter 1 only holds if the lawful uses are named, rather than negotiated case by case. This is the list — a trading business's legitimate journal traffic:

1. Accruals and prepayments. The matching principle's instruments (Chapter 4 works them fully): expenses spread to the periods that consumed them, income deferred to the periods that earned it. The largest lawful category, and monthly by nature.

2. Payroll. The salary journal from the payroll summary: DR salary expense (by department or dimension), CR net-pay liability (cleared by the payment run), CR the statutory custodies — PAYE, pension, other deductions — each a liability account holding money withheld for someone else. Where the payroll module automates this, the journal is machine-written; read it against the posting map once anyway. Module 5 covers the Nigerian statutory picture in full.

3. Depreciation. DR depreciation expense, CR accumulated depreciation — machine-written where the fixed-asset machinery runs (module 7), a governed monthly journal where it does not yet.

4. Bank charges, interest, and bank-side events. The charges the bank statement reveals: DR bank charges, CR bank — entered as Bank Entries with the statement as the reference, and only ever from the reconciliation (module 3), never from memory.

5. Opening balances. The go-live event: governed, evidenced, accountant-approved, and loaded once. The critical rule: opening debtors and creditors load as per-party, per-invoice detail — never one total posted to a control account. The tie must be born intact. Module 4 details the migration rules.

6. Owner and inter-entity movements. Capital introduced, drawings, director loans, movements between related entities — real events with no trading document. Journalised with the evidence referenced, with parties where applicable, and with the tax and legal shape decided by the accountant — this category most needs professional policy behind it.

7. Corrections. Lawful only under Chapter 5's rules.

The two tests. Whether a proposed journal belongs on this list comes down to:

1. The document test. Does a trading document exist for this event? If yes, the journal is forbidden regardless of convenience — the sale, the purchase, the stock move and the payment all have documents.
2. The evidence test. Can the journal name its paper — the agreement, the statement, the summary, the schedule? A journal that cannot reference evidence is an assertion, not an entry.

Practical rule: the lawful list for a given business fits on one page, and most of it recurs monthly. Chapter 7 turns that page into templates — after which anything outside the templates is, by construction, visible and reviewable.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Accruals and prepayments, worked
lessons.html:
The lawful list's largest resident gets its own chapter, because matching is the accounting idea most worth holding fluently, and its journals are the recurring set every implementation builds.

The principle. The P&L's job is to state what a period earned and what it consumed — not what it happened to pay. Cash timing and economic timing diverge constantly: rent paid yearly is consumed monthly; power consumed now is billed next month. Matching books each on its own date: the payment's date is a bank fact; the expense's date is a consumption fact. Without matching, margins lurch with payment calendars — the January that carries a whole year's rent, the fat months where no bills happened to arrive — and every monthly report reads noise.

Prepayment, worked. HealthTrade pays annual rent of ₦2,400,000 in January.

1. The payment: DR Prepaid Rent ₦2,400,000, CR Bank. Prepaid Rent is an asset — eleven months of future occupancy is a thing the business owns.
2. The monthly journal, twelve times: DR Rent Expense ₦200,000, CR Prepaid Rent ₦200,000 — each month consuming one-twelfth of the asset into expense.

Result: January's P&L carries ₦200,000 of rent, not ₦2.4m; December carries its ₦200,000 from cash paid a year earlier; and the Prepaid Rent balance at any month is the occupancy still owed — a balance-sheet line that means something. The recurring template (Chapter 7) writes this without anyone remembering, and the same shape serves insurance, licences and subscriptions — anything paid ahead of its consumption.

Accrual, worked. The mirror. March consumes ₦180,000 of diesel and power, but the bills arrive in April.

1. March's close journal: DR Utilities Expense ₦180,000, CR Accrued Expenses (a liability — the business owes for what it consumed). March's P&L now tells March's truth.
2. The reversal: the accrual reverses on April 1st — use the system's auto-reversal for exactly this.
3. April's actual bills post through their proper purchase documents. The reversal has already cleared the estimate, so the actuals land clean — no double-count.

The estimate → reverse → actual rhythm is the monthly craft. The close-checklist question that drives it: which consumptions have no bills yet?

The income side. The mirror mirrored: cash received ahead of earning is not income — it is a liability (unearned income) until the earning happens, then a journal moves it to income as it is earned. Deposits and retainers follow this shape.

Summary. Prepayment: pay into an asset, consume monthly into expense. Accrual: estimate the consumed-but-unbilled at close, auto-reverse on the 1st, let the actual documents land clean. Income received early: liability first, income as earned. Build all of it as templates; run it monthly, never annually.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The correction rules
lessons.html:
Mistakes happen — the wrong account, the wrong amount, the wrong month. What separates clean books from archaeology is how corrections are made. Four rules, no exceptions.

Rule 1 — history is never edited. A posted entry is a permanent record. Corrections are new entries that reverse and restate, standing beside the mistake forever, telling the full story: error, discovery, repair. Even where permissions technically allow amending a posted entry, do not — an edited past is a ledger that lies about its own history, and everyone who reconciles, audits or relies on the books depends on that never happening.

Rule 2 — reverse and repost. The mechanical form:

1. Post a reversing entry — the original's exact mirror: same accounts, same amounts, directions flipped. The system's reverse function builds it.
2. Post a fresh entry with the correct accounts and amounts.
3. Both carry references to the original and to each other, and remarks that narrate: reversal of JV-0231, expense posted to wrong account; see JV-0233 for correct posting.

The GL then reads mistake — mirror — truth: three entries, one honest story, reconstructable by any reviewer in a minute.

Rule 3 — documents are corrected as documents. The most-violated rule, and the one protecting everything module 1 built. When the error lives in a trading document — the invoice with the wrong customer, the receipt with the wrong quantity, the payment against the wrong reference — the correction happens at the document: cancel-and-amend where the chain allows, or the returns and credit/debit note machinery where trade has moved on. Never as a journal patching the GL around it.

Why: the journal patch fixes the balance while the document still tells the old story. The party ledger, the stock ledger, the tax register and the match queue now all disagree with a GL that looks right, and the standing agreements begin to diverge. The diagnostic that follows from this: a tie that will not reconcile almost always has a journal in it — and the fastest audit in accounting is filtering journals against the control, stock, tax and bank accounts, where honest journal traffic is nearly zero.

Rule 4 — the period decides the date. An error found in an open month is corrected in that month, honest-dated. An error found after the close is corrected in the current period, with remarks naming the original period and entry — closed months are not reopened for corrections. (Module 7 covers the close; module 8 covers the settings that enforce the freeze.)

Summary. Never edit; reverse and repost with cross-references and a story; correct documents at the document, never by journal; and date corrections by the period rule. Books kept this way remember both the mistake and the repair — which is exactly what makes them believable.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The forbidden list
lessons.html:
Some journals are not merely governed — they are forbidden, because each one breaks machinery that cannot report its own breakage. Learn the list with each entry's what breaks.

1. Revenue journals replacing invoices. DR Debtors, CR Sales, no invoice. Breaks: the VAT register (output tax unbooked or untracked — a compliance failure, not a style choice), the customer's document trail (a balance with no invoice to allocate, dispute or statement), collections (nothing ages properly), and e-invoicing obligations where they apply. The sale has a document; use it. The purchase-side twin is equally forbidden: expense journals replacing supplier invoices break input VAT, WHT capture and the creditor's ledger at once.

2. Journals to Stock accounts. Breaks: the stock-to-accounts agreement — the GL moves, the stock ledger does not, and the two diverge by exactly the journal's amount, permanently, until someone excavates. If stock value is wrong, the error is in a stock document — a receipt's rate, a missing entry, a reconciliation — find it and fix it there. The fence around Stock-type accounts exists for this paragraph.

3. Journals to control accounts. Without a party: forbidden outright — a naira belonging to no customer, the tie broken (module 1, Chapter 7). Even with a party, treat control-account journals with suspicion: the events they usually claim — write-offs, discounts, settlement adjustments — have proper instruments (credit and debit notes, payment deductions, bad-debt provisioning in module 4) that carry the tax and ledger consequences the bare journal skips. Working rule: control-account journals are rare, party-carrying, and second-approved — or they are the disease.

4. Journals to tax accounts outside the filing routine. Breaks: the register agreement — VAT Payable that no longer equals the invoice register's story; WHT accounts that no longer tie to certificates. Tax accounts move by documents and by the filing-and-remittance entries (module 5). The adjusting journal that forces the account to match a figure computed outside the system is backwards: reconcile the register, find the divergence, fix its document.

5. Journals to bank accounts outside real bank events. Breaks: the bank reconciliation — the GL bank balance acquires a line the statement will never show, and the reconciliation carries an unexplained item forever. Bank accounts move by payment entries, contra entries, and the reconciliation's own charge entries — nothing else.

The shared shape. Every item on this list is the same mistake: a total adjusted around its details. The GL looks right; the machinery beneath it now disagrees; and the disagreement surfaces later, further from its cause, more expensive to trace. When a standing agreement will not reconcile, filter the journals on that account family first — it is the fastest diagnosis in this track.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Journal controls: the narrow door
lessons.html:
Direct GL access is a dangerous power, and it gets the same treatment every dangerous power gets: named holders, thresholds, templates, and a monthly review.

Who may journal. Narrow: the accountant and one named backstop — two people, not two departments. Never warehouse or sales operators; never branch managers — their corrections route through documents and requests, not direct GL access. A journal can move any naira anywhere; the day everyone holds the pen, every fence in Chapter 6 becomes a suggestion.

Thresholds and second approval.

• Value thresholds route large journals to a second sign-off, even between the two named holders — the submission workflow carries it.
• Certain categories are second-approved regardless of value: anything touching control accounts (Chapter 6's rare-and-party-carrying rule, enforced as workflow), opening and closing entries, and corrections above the materiality line.
• The threshold numbers are the business's own decision, written in the policy notes like every other control number.

Templates for the recurring set. The lawful monthly traffic — accruals, prepayment consumptions, payroll, depreciation — is built once as templates: accounts pre-wired, dimensions pre-set, stories pre-written, amounts updated per period (or generated by the machinery where it runs). Two payoffs:

1. The template set is the manual layer's honest census — a trading business's recurring journals fit on one page.
2. Everything outside the templates is, by construction, an event: visible, reviewable, and asked about. The review question changes from are these thousand journals right? to the recurring set ran; what are these six others?

The monthly journal review. A standing line on the close checklist: every journal of the month, listed, read against five questions — author, accounts, direction, date, story. Ten to twenty minutes at a healthy business, because the count is small. The review reads in both directions:

• Individually: the forbidden account touched, the empty remarks, the date that wandered into the wrong period.
• In aggregate: the journal count trending up (the machine being declined); the same correction repeating (an upstream problem to fix at source); one author's entries clustering at period-end (a pattern that deserves a conversation).

Summary. Two named holders; thresholds and category-based second approval; the recurring set as one page of templates; and the monthly review — five questions per entry, both directions. Under these controls the journal is what it should be: a small, well-lit room instead of a back door.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's manual layer
lessons.html:
The month HealthTrade's manual layer was built, and the three tests that proved it. Every chapter of this module appears.

The recurring set built (Chapters 3-4, 7). The accountant and the implementation team census the genuine journal traffic and build the templates in an afternoon:

• Rent: the ₦2.4m January payment to Prepaid Rent; the ₦200,000 monthly consumption template, story pre-written, twelve months scheduled.
• Payroll: from the payroll summary — salary expense by dimension, net-pay liability, PAYE and pension custodies. Module 5's deep dive noted.
• Utilities accrual: the month-end estimate, auto-reversing on the 1st. The estimate-reverse-actual rhythm is demonstrated live across March and April: March's ₦180,000 accrual, April's automatic reversal, April's actual bills posting through purchase documents, the net landing clean. The accountant, seeing the reversal pattern work for the first time, adopts it for two more accrual lines unprompted.
• Depreciation: a governed monthly journal for now; the fixed-asset automation noted for module 7.

The census closes at seven recurring templates — one page, as Chapter 7 promised.

A correction done right (Chapter 5). Week three: February's generator maintenance — ₦340,000 — is discovered posted to Repairs, when policy wants it in the dedicated Generator Running Costs line the MD reads separately. The temptation to edit the posted entry is declined out loud, as teaching. Instead: the mirror reversal (referenced to the original), the fresh posting to the right account (referenced to both), remarks narrating all three. The GL reads mistake — mirror — truth, and the drill-down from the MD's generator line tells the whole story in four clicks. The accountant's comment: the books now remember the mistake and the repair — that is what makes them believable.

A forbidden journal refused (Chapter 6). Week four: a branch manager calls the accountant directly — a customer is disputing ₦86,000; just adjust the debtor and we'll sort it later. The refusal is the fence working: a journal to Debtors would move the control while no document tells the customer's ledger why — the statement would show a naked adjustment and the dispute would lose its paper trail. The routing instead: the dispute is investigated, resolves as a pricing error on one line, and a credit note is issued for the difference — which corrects the balance, the VAT, and the customer's statement in one instrument. The manager gets the outcome he wanted; the books get it the right way.

Month end (Chapter 7). The first monthly journal review runs: the seven templates fired on schedule, plus four other journals — each read against the five questions, one bounced back for empty remarks and resubmitted with its story. Total review time: fourteen minutes. The journal count is noted as the layer's standing health figure.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the second law
lessons.html:
The manual layer's recurring failures. Symptom, cause, fix — and the review list.

Pattern 1 — the journal habit. Symptom: hundreds of journals monthly; sales and purchases journalised; the trading modules idle. Cause: fluency in manual books never transferred to the system (Chapter 1). Fix: apply the document test to the whole traffic; migrate the biggest categories to their documents first — sales, then purchases, then payments; teach the transfer with respect; and watch the journal count as the recovery's measure.

Pattern 2 — suspense parking. Symptom: the balancing side nobody could find, parked in suspense; the account growing monthly. Cause: the one-sided instinct — posting what is known and warehousing the rest (Chapter 2). Fix: take the balance rule seriously (the other side always exists — find it or do not post), sweep suspense to zero monthly, and fix the classification gaps at their source.

Pattern 3 — the tie-breaker journals. Symptom: control accounts that stopped agreeing with their parties; a stock agreement diverged by a suspiciously round number; a tax account that matches a filing but not its register. Cause: the forbidden list violated — totals adjusted around their details (Chapter 6). Fix: filter journals on the protected accounts (the fastest audit in this track), reverse each hit and re-route it through its proper instrument, re-teach the fence, and narrow the door.

Pattern 4 — the storyless journal. Symptom: entries whose remarks are empty, cryptic, or say adjustment; reviews that stall on them; authors who cannot recall them. Cause: the remarks rule unenforced (Chapter 2). Fix: require the story at entry, bounce storyless journals back in the monthly review, and let templates carry pre-written stories so routine traffic is never the problem.

Pattern 5 — the year-end journal storm. Symptom: a quiet ledger all year, then fifty journals in the close week — accruals never run monthly, corrections hoarded, adjustments landing in one avalanche. Cause: the manual layer run annually instead of monthly (Chapters 4, 7) — every month's statements wrong all year, corrected once, when nobody remembers anything. Fix: the recurring set on its monthly rhythm, corrections posted when found, the monthly review keeping the layer current.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can state: what the journal bypasses and why the break is silent; the fields and their rules (balance, party, date, type, reference, remarks); the lawful list and the two tests; the prepayment and accrual worked examples and the estimate-reverse-actual rhythm; the four correction rules; the forbidden list with what each breaks; and the controls — two holders, thresholds, templates, the five-question monthly review.

The second law: the journal is the exception and the document is the rule — what a document can do, a document must do. Module 3 takes the books to their outside witness: the bank.

banking.title: Accounts 3 — Banking & Reconciliation
banking.desc: Banking and reconciliation: the bank statement as the record the business does not write, the account and payment-mode wiring, the monthly matching routine with the reconciliation equation, the three remainder categories with written age limits, the imprest float and its invariant, the four-link retail cash-up chain, and bank governance — prepare/release separation, masters-not-messages, and the mandate review.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The outside witness
lessons.html:
Every check so far compared the business's records with each other. This module's check is stronger, because one side of it is a record the business does not write: the bank statement. The reconciliation that examines it monthly is accounting's most important routine, and this module covers it end to end — the setup, the matching, the differences, cash handling, the retail cash-up chain, and bank governance.

Why the outside record matters. Internal records can share a disease: the same wrong default poisons the invoice and the register together; the same fraud writes both sides of its own story. The bank's record cannot be reached by any of it. The statement says what money actually moved, when, and where. Every internal money record ultimately settles against the statement, and a business whose books reconcile to its banks monthly has anchored its whole financial story to a record nobody inside the building can edit. A business whose books do not reconcile has an unanchored story — whatever else it has.

What reconciliation is. The disciplined comparison: every statement line matched to a GL entry, every GL bank entry matched to a statement line, and the unmatched remainder named, explained, and worked (Chapters 3-4). Three things it is not:

• Not a formality — a tick-and-file that examines nothing proves nothing.
• Not a plug — a balancing journal that forces agreement hides every real difference. Chapter 9 treats the plug as this module's most serious failure.
• Not optional at any size — the two-person business and the hundred-branch network reconcile for the same reasons, and the cost — about an hour per bank per month at a healthy business — is the cheapest error and fraud detection available.

What the unreconciled business cannot know. Whether its cash position is real (decisions made on a GL balance the bank disagrees with are decisions made on fiction). Whether payments landed (the transfer that failed silently; the cheque never presented). What the bank has been taking (charges and deductions accumulating unbooked). And whether anyone is helping themselves — the classic frauds (the intercepted payment, the altered beneficiary, the takings banked short) are all caught first at reconciliation, or not at all.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the setup — bank accounts and payment modes. Chapter 3: the matching routine. Chapter 4: working the differences. Chapter 5: cash — the float and the imprest system. Chapter 6: the retail cash-up chain, from drawer to statement. Chapter 7: bank governance. Chapter 8: HealthTrade's banking year. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Bank accounts and payment modes
lessons.html:
Reconciliation needs the wiring right first: the real-world banks represented so the machinery can see them.

One real account, one leaf. Every actual bank account — each with its own statement — is its own Bank-type ledger account:

• Typed Bank, so the reconciliation machinery can see it (module 1's type rule).
• Named plainly for the long term: GTB Current - 0123, not Bank 2.
• Grouped under Bank Accounts for the rollup read.
• Paired with its bank account record — the master carrying the account number, branch, and reconciliation linkage — created together with the leaf.

Two refusals follow from the rule: never pool two real accounts into one leaf (two statements cannot reconcile against one ledger), and never split one real account across leaves.

Payment modes. The Mode of Payment is the front-line vocabulary — Cash, Transfer, POS, Cheque — and each mode maps to the account the money truly lands in: Transfer to the receiving bank leaf, Cash to the cash account, POS to the settlement path Chapter 6 covers. A mis-mapped mode is the quiet disease this chapter exists to prevent: every payment taken on it posts to the wrong leaf, one bank's reconciliation inherits a stream of phantom entries and another's misses a stream of real ones — weeks of tangle from one dropdown. Verify the mode map at go-live, and re-walk it whenever banks change.

Movements between own accounts. Cash banked, funds shifted between banks, the float replenished — these are contra entries (module 2's type): one leaf credited, the other debited, no income or expense anywhere; the business is moving money between its own pockets. The discipline is the pairing: a contra touches two reconcilable worlds — the sending statement and the receiving one (or the cash count) — and both sides must land. The transfer is recorded when initiated, matched on the sending statement when it leaves, matched on the receiving statement when it arrives, and the in-transit gap (initiated Friday, landed Monday) lives as a timing item both reconciliations can see. Chapter 4 ages it.

Multiple banks, deliberately. Businesses hold several banks for real reasons — clearing relationships, lending, branch cash handling. Keep the purposes written: each account's job noted on its record (operating, tax reserve, payroll), so the account list stays a design rather than an accumulation, and the annual review can ask whether each account still earns its place.

Summary. One real account per typed leaf, plainly named, paired with its record; every payment mode mapped to its true landing account and verified at go-live; own-account movements as contras with both sides matched; and each bank's purpose written down.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The reconciliation routine
lessons.html:
The reconciliation itself: monthly, per account, from the statement's own cutoff date.

The frame. Two lists face each other: the statement's lines for the period, and the GL bank account's entries. The goal is total mutual accounting — every statement line matched to a ledger entry, every ledger entry matched to a statement line — with the two closing balances tied together through the explained remainder. The classic arithmetic: GL balance + deposits the bank has not yet seen − payments the bank has not yet cleared = statement balance. When that equation closes with every remaining item named, the account is reconciled. When it closes only through an unexplained difference, it is not reconciled — it is approximately narrated, which is a different thing.

The matching pass. Run from easiest to hardest:

1. Exact amount-and-date pairs — the bulk: transfers and deposits that behaved.
2. Amount matches with date drift — the clearance lag: the payment entered Tuesday appears on the statement Thursday. Match them, and record the clearance date on the ledger entry — the field that marks an entry as witnessed, and the anchor for every uncleared-items report afterwards.
3. Composites — one statement line covering several ledger entries (the batched deposit), or one ledger entry split across several statement lines (the split settlement).
4. The remainder — whatever stays unmatched on either side. This is not a failure; it is the routine's actual product: the worklist Chapter 4 takes over.

Naming the remainder. Every surviving item belongs to one of three categories:

• Timing items (business side) — recorded by the business, not yet seen by the bank: the cheque issued and unpresented, the transfer in transit, the deposit lodged after the cutoff. Legitimate and expected — and aged (Chapter 4): a timing item that stops being timely stops being a timing item.
• Bank-side items, unbooked — seen by the bank, not yet recorded by the business: charges, interest, direct debits, standing orders, reversals, the customer who paid straight into the account unannounced. The reconciliation is where the business learns of these, and Chapter 4 books them from here — never from memory.
• Errors — either side's: the business's mis-keyed amount (corrected by module 2's rules), or — rare but real — the bank's own error, queried with the bank and tracked until reversed. Never absorbed.

Practical rules. Reconcile from the statement's cutoff, not a convenient date. Work one account at a time to completion. And finish every session with the remainder list written: item, category, amount, age, owner. A reconciliation whose output is that list has done its job; one whose output is a tick has done nothing.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Working the differences
lessons.html:
The remainder is named; now it is worked — each category's handling, plus the aging discipline that stops the reconciliation becoming a museum of old differences.

Timing items: ride, then investigate. The unpresented cheque and the in-transit transfer ride to next month's reconciliation, where most clear. The discipline is the age limit, written per instrument:

• Cheques — the validity window. A cheque unpresented at six months is stale by banking practice and must be resolved, not carried: contact the payee; if the cheque was lost or never received, reverse its ledger entry by the correction rules (with references) and reissue the payment properly.
• Transfers — days, not months. A transfer in transit beyond a week is not in transit; it is missing. Trace it with the bank; find or force the reversal.
• Deposits — the loudest alarm in the module: a lodged deposit missing from the statement is escalated same day. Chapter 6's chain names who carried it.

The uncleared-items report, aged, is the reconciliation's standing output — and a remainder list that only grows is Chapter 9's pattern in its early form.

Bank-side items: book from the statement. Charges, interest, direct debits, reversals — booked as Bank Entries, from the reconciliation, with the statement line referenced. That is the only lawful source: the bank account moves because the bank moved it, and the statement is the evidence. Two disciplines ride along:

• Reasonableness. Charges are read, not just booked — the charge schedule against the bank mandate. Banks err, and the business that books blindly subsidises the errors. A quarterly charges read against expectation is a small routine with a real yield.
• The unexplained credit. Money arriving unannounced is not income until identified. Park it as identified-pending, run the party investigation — it is usually a customer paying without a reference, resolved through the receivables machinery so the allocation lands properly. Never swallow it into income out of relief.

Errors: the correction rules, applied. Business-side errors surface here constantly — the transposed amount, the payment posted to the wrong bank leaf, the double entry. Every one corrects by module 2's rules: reverse and repost with references and remarks; and where a document erred, correct the document. The reconciliation's job is finding them; the correction rules' job is fixing them without rewriting history.

Summary. Timing items ride under written age limits and are investigated at the limit — cheque by its validity, transfer by the week, missing deposit same-day. Bank-side items book only from the statement, with a quarterly reasonableness read and unexplained credits parked, never pocketed. Errors correct by the rules. The aged remainder list is the standing output, and its length and age are the reconciliation's quality gauge.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Cash: the float and the imprest system
lessons.html:
The statement witnesses electronic money. Physical cash has no outside witness at all — which is why its rules are stricter and older.

Cash accounts: few, and owned. A Cash-type leaf for each real cash custody — the main cash account, each petty cash float — never one diffuse Cash account that several drawers share. Pooled custody is no custody: when several people share one cash balance, no variance can be attributed to anyone. Each custody has a named holder, a counting rhythm, and a written purpose. And the design goal is minimisation: cash custodies are attack surface, and Nigeria's transfer-heavy payment reality is an ally — fewer drawers, smaller floats, faster banking, less to defend.

The imprest float. Petty cash runs on the imprest system — the design that makes small cash self-controlling:

1. A fixed float (say ₦100,000) held by a named custodian.
2. Every disbursement against a voucher — what, why, who, with the receipt attached.
3. Replenishment reimburses exactly the vouchers' total, restoring the float to its fixed level.

The invariant that makes it work: cash in the box plus vouchers in the box equals the float, at every moment. A spot count takes two minutes and either ties or tells. Replenishment is where the accounting happens — the vouchers booked to their expense accounts, by dimension, in one entry, with the reimbursement transfer as the bank-side event. The GL stays clean of dribbles while every kobo stays evidenced.

The cash count. Scheduled counts (the float monthly; tills daily — Chapter 6) plus unscheduled spot counts — unpredictability is what keeps a counting programme honest. Counted by someone other than the custodian where the roster allows, against the invariant, with the standard variance rules: named the same day, investigated before adjusted, reason-coded, and read as a rate per custody over time. And the framing that matters for the people: the count protects the honest holder — the clean-count record is the custodian's own evidence. A custodian who welcomes spot counts is telling you something, as is one who resents them.

Cash rules, itemised.

• Disbursements only against vouchers — no IOUs living in the box; an IOU is an unauthorised loan wearing a scrap of paper.
• The float is fixed — topping it up by feel breaks the invariant.
• A spending cap routes anything substantial to the proper payment machinery, where it gets evidence and approval.
• Custodian changes are a counted handover: outgoing count, incoming count, both signed, same day.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The cash-up chain: drawer to statement
lessons.html:
Retail's daily money routine — the chain from the till drawer to the bank statement — is where more small money is lost than anywhere else in trade. The chain has four links, and each one is signed.

Link 1 — the till session. Each till, each day or shift, is a session: opened with a counted float, traded through the till's machinery (every sale a document), closed with a counted drawer. The session is the accountability unit — one till, one operator, one reconciliation. A pooled till (several operators, one drawer) converts every variance into an argument, which is why it is refused.

Link 2 — the cash-up. At session close:

1. The drawer is counted by denomination — the count sheet by note, because roughly ₦180k is not a count.
2. The count is compared against the system's session totals by mode: cash sales against cash in the drawer (less the float); POS-terminal sales against the terminal's settlement report; transfers against the transfer log.
3. Variances are named tonight, same day, while memory serves. A ₦14,000 short investigated at close is a training catch; discovered a week later it is an argument; a month later, a write-off.

Cash-up variances are read as a rate per till and per operator — rotating operators across tills separates the till from the person where a pattern appears — and the clean-session streak is the operator's own visible record.

Link 3 — banking the takings. Cash does not sleep in drawers:

• Banked intact — the whole count, never the count minus informal spendings. Takings that detour into expenses break the tie between till total and deposit slip, and every informal spend is an undocumented one.
• Banked fast — daily or next morning per policy and geography, the overnight safe's contents minimal.
• The deposit: counted, sealed, slipped, carried by a named person, lodged — and the deposit slip's amount must equal the cash-up's banked figure to the naira, because the next link checks it.

Link 4 — the statement closes the loop. The deposit appears on the bank statement, and the reconciliation (Chapter 3) matches it. The full chain: till total → cash-up → deposit slip → statement line — one unbroken sequence of agreeing numbers, each link signed by its custodian. When the chain breaks, the break names its link: a till-to-cash-up gap is a session problem; a cash-up-to-slip gap happened in counting or carriage; a slip-to-statement gap is the same-day alarm from Chapter 4.

Summary. One operator per session; denominated counts compared by mode, variances named tonight; takings banked intact and fast by named carriage; the statement matched at reconciliation. Four links, four signatures, one agreeing number end to end.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Bank governance
lessons.html:
Stock walks out in cartons; bank money leaves at wire speed. This chapter assembles the controls that defend it.

The release separation. The preparer of a payment — who assembles what to pay from system evidence — is never its releaser — who authorises it at the bank. And the payment run pays what the ledger supports: approved invoices, matched documents — never what a message asks. The separation survives every size of business because it is two people, not two departments: at eleven people, the founder releases what the accountant prepares.

Masters, not messages. The beneficiary-fraud defence:

• Payments go to the account details in the supplier master — never to details supplied in a message.
• Changes to those details are a governed master-data event: verified through a known channel back to a known person — never the phone number in the requesting email.
• The urgent message asking otherwise — the MD's spoofed mailbox, the supplier's lookalike domain, the WhatsApp that sounds exactly right — dies against the process. That is the point of having one.

The accounts team is this fraud's chosen target, because they hold the pen that pays. Refresh the training annually, and treat reported near-misses as wins, not embarrassments.

Mandates and signatories. The bank-side mirror of the system's permissions: who may sign, at what thresholds, in what combinations — kept aligned with the internal release design. A mandate broader than the internal control is a back door; one narrower is a bottleneck. Review the mandate on the annual walk and at every personnel change: the departed signatory is removed the week they leave, not the year — a stale mandate is a standing invitation. Online banking gets the same treatment in modern clothes: users named, limits set, tokens held personally, and the admin rights themselves held by two named people.

The bank calendar. The recurring lines this module adds:

• Monthly: the reconciliation, per account — with a written maximum tolerable unreconciled age (an account two months unreconciled is an incident, not a backlog); the uncleared-items aging read.
• Quarterly: the charges reasonableness read.
• Annually and on change: the mandate and online-user review.
• Per their schedules: the cash counts (Chapter 5) and till sessions (Chapter 6).
• Daily, where cash flow is tight: the cash position read across the banks.

Summary. Prepare and release separated; beneficiaries paid from masters with governed changes; mandates aligned, reviewed, and purged the week people leave; and the calendar — monthly reconciliation with a maximum age, quarterly charges read, annual mandate walk.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's banking year
lessons.html:
The outside witness, installed and lived. Every chapter appears.

The wiring and the first reconciliation (Chapters 2-4). Three banks become three typed leaves with written purposes — operating, tax reserve, payroll — and the mode map is verified (module 1's go-live check had already caught one mis-mapping). Then the hardest hour of the whole setup: the first reconciliation of the operating account, facing eighteen months of never-reconciled history. The dig, run once, properly: the matching pass leaves a remainder of 34 items, and worked by category it resolves into:

• A nine-month-old stale cheque — ₦210,000 to a supplier who never presented it. The payee is contacted (the cheque was lost), the ledger entry reversed by the correction rules with references, and the payment reissued through the proper run.
• An unbooked charges trail — fourteen months of charges and levies never entered, booked in one referenced sitting. The reasonableness read then finds two duplicate charges, queried and recovered from the bank: ₦38,000 back.
• One mis-mapped POS week — settlements posted to the wrong bank leaf during a terminal change. Corrected by the rules; the mode map fixed.
• An unexplained credit of ₦127,000 — parked identified-pending, traced within the week to a customer who paid without a reference, and allocated through receivables so the tie held.

Month two's reconciliation takes fifty minutes. Month three's, forty.

The float installed (Chapter 5). The office's drawer-of-mystery becomes a ₦100,000 imprest float: named custodian, voucher pad, the invariant taught — cash plus vouchers equals one hundred, always — and monthly replenishment through the payment machinery with vouchers booked by dimension. The first unscheduled spot count, week three, ties to the naira, and the custodian asks when the next one is. Unscheduled, comes the answer — the system working.

The cash-up chain (Chapter 6). Till sessions start at the retail counter: opening floats, denominated closing counts, mode-split cash-up. Day nine catches the chain's first fish: the evening count is ₦14,000 short against cash sales — named that night, investigated while memory serves, and resolved as two transfer-paid sales rung as cash by a new operator. A mode error, not a theft: the sessions are corrected by document, the operator trained, and the variance rate returns to zero. Takings bank intact next morning by named carriage; the slips match the cash-ups to the naira; the statement matches the slips — the chain closes its loop for the first full month.

Governance (Chapter 7). The mandate review finds a former manager still a signatory eight months after leaving — removed the same week, and the personnel-change trigger added to the leaver checklist. The prepare/release separation is confirmed live: the accountant prepares the run; the MD releases it. The year ends with three banks reconciling in under two hours total per month, and the MD's note: I used to check the bank app and hope. Now the books and the bank argue it out monthly, and I read the result.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the third law
lessons.html:
The banking layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the never-reconciled account. Symptom: a GL bank balance nobody would bet on; decisions made on it anyway; the statement opened only to see if a payment landed. Cause: the outside record never examined (Chapters 1, 3). Fix: the first-dig reconciliation — priced honestly, it faces the whole history once — then the monthly rhythm, with the maximum-unreconciled-age policy making relapse an incident.

Pattern 2 — reconciliation by plug. Symptom: accounts that reconcile perfectly every month via a balancing journal to reconciliation differences or suspense. Cause: the module's most serious failure — forcing agreement converts every real difference (error, fraud, drift) into a booked fiction, and the account looks reconciled precisely because it never is. Fix: excavate the plug account's history (each plugged amount is an unworked difference), forbid the plug, and install the name-every-item discipline. An unexplained difference carried openly is honest; one booked away is not.

Pattern 3 — the museum remainder. Symptom: uncleared items riding for a year; stale cheques immortal; in-transit items old enough to walk. Cause: the aging discipline absent (Chapter 4). Fix: age limits written per instrument, the monthly aging read with investigation at the limit, and the remainder list's length and age on the close checklist as the reconciliation's quality gauge.

Pattern 4 — cash counted never. Symptom: the drawer of mystery; IOUs in the float; petty cash topped up by feel; variances discovered annually and absorbed silently. Cause: the no-witness asset given no discipline either (Chapter 5). Fix: the imprest installed (the invariant makes counting trivial), custodies named and minimal, the count rhythm with spot checks, and the spending cap routing real expenses to the evidenced machinery.

Pattern 5 — the leaking chain. Symptom: till totals, cash-ups, deposit slips and statement lines each telling a slightly different number; takings banked late and light; variance arguments a week after the fact. Cause: the chain's links unsigned (Chapter 6) — pooled tills, undenominated counts, informal spendings en route, unnamed carriage. Fix: sessions and same-day cash-ups, intact and fast banking by named carriage, and the four-link match run monthly at reconciliation.

The review list. Confirm you can state: why the outside record is categorically stronger; the wiring rules (one account one leaf, the mode map, contras); the matching order and the reconciliation equation; the three remainder categories and each one's handling with its age limit; the imprest invariant and the cash rules; the four links of the cash-up chain and what each break means; and the governance set — prepare/release, masters-not-messages, mandates aligned and purged.

The third law: every bank account is reconciled monthly, and every difference is named — never plugged. Module 4 turns to the promises: receivables and payables from the accounts chair.
