ar_ap_chair.title: Accounts 4 — Receivables & Payables from the Accounts Chair
ar_ap_chair.desc: Receivables and payables from the accounts chair: the record kept real, collectable, current and complete — the monthly tie check, the unallocated read worked to near-zero, advances in both directions under the never-net rule, provisioning by aging matrix with governed write-offs and recoveries, statements and confirmations with the supplier-statement mirror, detail-never-blobs migration, and the ninety-minute month-end ritual.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The accounts chair: owning the record
lessons.html:
The sales desk runs credit control and collections; the purchasing desk runs the invoice match and the payment run. This module sits in a third chair — the accounts chair — and its distinction is one sentence: the trading desks own the relationships; the accounts chair owns the record — its integrity, its honesty, and what it asserts to everyone who reads the balance sheet.

The two promise lines. Debtors and Creditors are the balance sheet's promise accounts: money the world owes the business, and money the business owes the world. They are usually the largest figures after stock — and unlike stock, which can be physically counted, a receivable is only as real as its record. No shelf holds it; its entire existence is the party's ledger, the documents behind it, and the tie that proves the total. Someone must own that bookkeeping with the same rigor the warehouse owns the shelves. This module is that ownership, made operational.

The chair's first duty: the tie. Module 1 built the control-to-party tie; this module operates it: checked monthly (control balance against the party report's sum, to the kobo — Chapter 7 schedules it), divergences treated as incidents with the journal filter as the first tool. Every discipline in the chapters ahead is tie maintenance in some form: allocation hygiene keeps the details telling their story cleanly (Chapter 2), provisioning keeps the total honest about collectability (Chapter 4), confirmations test the record against the world (Chapter 5), and migration decides whether the tie is born intact or born broken (Chapter 6).

The four questions. The trading desks read these balances operationally — who to chase, who to pay. The accounts chair reads them as assertions. The balance sheet says ₦18.4m is receivable. Is it:

• Real — every naira party-attached and document-backed?
• Collectable — the provision question: ₦18.4m gross of which ₦1.2m is doubtful is a different assertion.
• Current — the aging honest, advances not netted against debts (Chapter 3's rule)?
• Complete — nothing quietly deleted, nothing parked off-ledger?

Four adjectives — real, collectable, current, complete — and an auditor's entire receivables programme is those four questions asked systematically. A chair that keeps them answered all year meets any audit calmly.

Module contents. Chapter 2: allocation hygiene. Chapter 3: advances, both directions. Chapter 4: provisioning and bad debts. Chapter 5: statements and confirmations. Chapter 6: opening balances and migration. Chapter 7: the month-end ritual. Chapter 8: HealthTrade's year in the chair. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Allocation hygiene: the unallocated read
lessons.html:
Allocation is taught at the payment desks; the accounts chair inherits what the desks leave behind. This chapter is the standing cleanup that keeps party ledgers legible.

What unallocated means. A party's ledger is entries; a party's story is entries matched — this payment against these invoices, this credit note applied to that invoice, this advance consumed by that bill. Every unmatched item is a naira of ambiguity:

• The payment-on-account sitting against no invoice: which debts does it settle? Until someone says, the aging lies — the invoices it should have cleared still age as unpaid while the ledger's net looks fine.
• The credit note issued and never applied: the customer's statement shows a debt and a floating credit side by side — and the customer, reasonably, pays the net and disputes the rest.
• The advance unmatched — Chapter 3's whole subject.

The balance can be right while the story is illegible, and illegible stories rot statements, aging reports, collections priorities, and eventually the relationship — because every conversation starts with twenty minutes of archaeology.

The unallocated read. The standing report: unallocated payments, unapplied credit notes, unmatched advances — per party, aged, valued. Read monthly (Chapter 7 schedules it) and worked to near-zero. Each item is:

1. Matched — allocated against its invoices, driven from the accounts side; where the intent is genuinely unknown, the customer is asked: your payment of the 14th — against which invoices? A professional question that also quietly tells the customer their account is watched.
2. Refunded — the genuine overpayment returned through the proper payment machinery.
3. Escalated — the item nobody can explain after honest work. Rare, and exactly what the chair exists to chase down rather than let ride.

Why near-zero compounds. Kept near-zero: every statement is self-explanatory, every aging line is a real debt, every collections call starts from agreed facts, and the monthly tie check is trivial. Lapsed for two quarters: the aging overstates (unallocated credits hide inside net balances), collections chase already-paid debts (the relationship cost), statements teach customers to dispute (the training cost), and the cleanup becomes a project instead of a routine.

Practical rule: grade each month's allocation discipline by the list's length. A growing unallocated report is the earliest warning this module gives, and it costs one glance to read.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Advances, both directions
lessons.html:
Money moves ahead of documents in both directions — customers pay before invoices; the business pays suppliers before bills. Advances are where promise accounting gets subtle, and both directions run on one discipline.

Customer advances: the liability. Cash received ahead of earning is not income, and not a negative receivable left to confuse the aging — it is a liability: the business owes goods, services, or the money back. The handling:

1. Captured as an advance — the payment entry flagged, the liability posting where the configuration routes it.
2. Matched to its invoice when the trade completes — the advance consumed, the liability extinguished, the invoice settled in one motion.
3. Reported as what it is — the never-net rule below.

The advance left unmatched after its trade completed is Chapter 2's problem in its most expensive form: the customer who paid ahead and got invoiced now shows a debt and a credit nobody joined — and pays neither attention.

Supplier advances: the asset, and the known black hole. The advance paid to a supplier is an asset (a prepayment — the business owns a claim), matched against the supplier's invoice when it lands, and aged while it waits. The advances-aging report — per supplier, valued, dated against expected delivery — is the chair's standing lamp over the classic failure: the advance paid, the goods arriving, and the bill settled again because nobody matched. Two structural defences:

• An advance aging past its expected delivery is either a late supplier (an expediting conversation) or a lost claim compounding quietly — the monthly aging decides which.
• The invoice-entry step checks for open advances before settlement — a workflow habit the chair audits, because the advance the payment run does not know about is the one that gets paid twice.

The reporting rule: never net. The subtle sin this chapter forbids: netting — a customer's advance netted against debts into one rolled figure, or advances buried inside the receivables line so the balance sheet shows ₦18.4m receivable when the truth is ₦19.6m owed-to-us and ₦1.2m owed-by-us. The two directions are different assertions (an asset and a liability), different risks, and different tax stories. The statements show them separately, always. The reader's test: can a banker see the real position from the face of the statement?

Summary. Customer advances: liability at capture, consumed at invoice, never left floating. Supplier advances: asset at capture, aged against expected delivery, checked before every settlement. Both directions: anchored to expected dates, reviewed monthly, and never netted in reporting.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Provisioning and bad debts
lessons.html:
Some promises break. The chair's hardest duty is saying so — in the books, on a policy, before anyone asks. The doctrine: doubtful, provided, written off, and sometimes recovered.

The two stages.

• Doubtful. Collection is uncertain — the customer silent past every escalation, disputing without engaging, visibly distressed. Response: a provision — an estimate of the loss, charged now: DR bad-debt expense, CR provision for doubtful debts (a contra-asset sitting against gross receivables). The debt itself stays on the party's ledger, and collections keeps working it.
• Bad. Collection has failed definitively — the customer wound up, vanished, or pursuit costs more than the claim per policy. Response: the write-off — the debt removed from the party ledger against the provision (or straight to expense where unprovided), governed like every destruction of value: evidence documented (the chase history), approvals by threshold (two names, value-routed), the tax notes captured (deductibility has conditions — the accountant owns them), and the party's record retained: written off is not erased; the history survives for the day the customer returns wanting credit.

The provision policy: a matrix, not a mood. The provision's size is an estimate, and estimates need policy or they become tuning knobs. The standard instrument is the aging matrix — provision percentages by age band, for example: 0-60 days nil, 61-120 at 10%, 121-180 at 25%, 181-365 at 50%, over a year at 100%. The numbers are the accountant's policy call, informed by the business's actual collection history; the structure is universal. Two adjustments ride on top:

• The large debt with specific bad news is provided specifically, regardless of age.
• The aged debt with a signed payment plan performing on schedule can be relieved judgmentally — the matrix is the floor; judgment documents its exceptions.

The mechanics each period. The matrix is applied to the fresh aging; the entry adjusts the provision to the required level — up as a charge, down as a release — and the movement, not the balance, is what the P&L reader sees. This is why the policy must be stable: a provision moved by policy is information (collections got worse, or better); one moved by discretion is noise at best.

Recoveries. A written-off debt sometimes pays. The recovery lands as income through the payment machinery, referenced end to end — and it lands cleanly precisely because the party's record survived the write-off. Chapter 8 shows HealthTrade's own case.

Summary. Doubtful → provision by matrix, debt stays and is chased. Bad → write-off on two signatures with evidence, record retained. Policy stable, movements explained, exceptions documented, recoveries through the machinery.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Statements and confirmations
lessons.html:
The party ledger faces the world through four routines: the statement run, on-record dispute handling, the audit confirmation, and the supplier-statement reconciliation.

The statement run. The customer statement is the party ledger, printed: monthly, to every open-balance customer, showing the period's documents, payments, allocations, and the aged balance. The run is cheap — the machinery formats what allocation hygiene keeps legible — and it returns three things:

1. Collections pressure — the statement is the chase's ambient reminder.
2. Free error-surfacing — customers audit their statements: the missed payment, the unapplied credit, the invoice they never received all come back as queries, and each one is tie maintenance done for you.
3. Dispute hygiene — disagreements handled on record: the disputed line flagged in the system, the resolution documented, and the correcting instrument (credit note, allocation, or a firm restatement of the debt) issued as a document. Never as side-agreements living in someone's inbox — the side-agreement is the statement's silent contradiction and an audit's favourite finding.

The audit confirmation. The external audit's receivables centrepiece: the auditor selects parties, sends balance confirmations, and compares the replies to the ledger. A chair that ran this module's disciplines meets it calmly — balances party-attached and document-backed (real), provisions on policy (collectable), advances un-netted (current), nothing deleted (complete). The four adjectives, pre-answered. One courtesy helps: warn the selected customers that confirmations are coming — an expected confirmation gets a reply; an ignored one costs a follow-up cycle.

The mirror: supplier statement reconciliation. The payables side has its own near-outside witness: the supplier's statement of your account, reconciled against your creditor ledger. Not as independent as the bank — the supplier writes it, and suppliers err in both directions — but structurally the same routine: their lines matched to your entries, the remainder named. The catches it makes:

• Invoices they show that you never received — the missing-bill catch: a liability that exists in the world but not in your books, found before it arrives as a surprise demand.
• Credit notes they issued that you never captured — money owed to you, sitting unclaimed.
• Payments you made that they never applied — the allocation conversation, from the other side.

Run it monthly for the top suppliers, on rotation for the rest (Chapter 7 schedules it).

Summary. Statements monthly to every open balance; disputes on record with document instruments; confirmations met with the four adjectives pre-answered; and the supplier statements reconciled — the mirror that catches missing bills and unclaimed credits.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Opening balances and migration
lessons.html:
Every AR/AP ledger was born somewhere — usually in a migration weekend — and how it was born decides whether the chair inherits a working tie or an archaeology site.

The loading rule: detail, never blobs. Opening receivables load per party, per open document: each customer's balance decomposed into its actual open invoices — numbers, dates, amounts, due dates from the old records — entered so that:

• The new system's aging is true from day one — every balance ages from its real invoice date, not from go-live.
• Every future payment has real invoices to allocate against — Chapter 2's hygiene is possible at all.
• The tie is born intact — the control equals the sum of real party detail.

The blob alternative — one opening balance per customer, or worst of all one journal to the Debtors control — is the tie born broken: a total with no details, an aging that starts blind (collections priorities scrambled for a year), and an allocation machinery with nothing to match (every payment on-account forever). The same rule mirrors to payables: per supplier, per open bill — the payment run's evidence and the supplier-statement reconciliation both need documents, not assertions.

The mechanics.

• Use the opening instruments the setup provides — opening invoice tools, or governed journals per party per document — posting against the opening equity account so the openings do not fabricate revenue or expense in year one.
• Date with the true original dates where the aging must be honest; where the system's opening pattern forces posting-date compromises, preserve the due dates — the accountant's call, documented.
• Advances load as advances — never netted into balances; Chapter 3's rule applies from day one.
• Disputed balances load flagged — the dispute history summarised, not laundered by migration.
• Provisions load as the policy's opening position — the matrix applied to the opening aging, so the honesty doctrine is born with the ledger rather than retrofitted at the first year-end.

The migration reconciliation. The proof, before go-live is called done:

1. The new system's control balances tie to the old system's (or the signed trial balance's) totals to the kobo.
2. The new party sums tie to the old party listings.
3. The differences — there are always differences — are worked to zero or documented as deliberate corrections: the old system's known errors fixed at migration, listed, and signed off.

Practical rule: price the detailed load honestly at planning time. It costs days where the blob costs hours — and the blob's true price is a year of blind aging, permanent on-account payments, and a tie that never agreed. The detail is the cheap option; it just pays upfront.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The month-end AR/AP ritual
lessons.html:
The chair's disciplines, assembled into one monthly sitting. Ninety minutes at a healthy business, one owner, one list — run in this order:

1. The tie check — first, always. Debtors control against the customer balance sum; Creditors against the supplier sum; to the kobo. Agreement: one line, initialed, done — two minutes. Divergence: an incident — run the journal filter first (the answer is almost always a journal), find the offending entry, correct it by the rules, and never carry the divergence forward unexplained.

2. The unallocated sweep. Chapter 2's read: unallocated payments, unapplied credits, per party, aged. Worked to near-zero; the escalations named. The month's allocation discipline is graded by this list's length.

3. The advance aging — both directions. Customer advances against their expected completions; supplier advances against expected deliveries. Items aged past plausibility resolved or escalated; the never-net rule confirmed in the reporting.

4. The provision review. The matrix run against the fresh aging; the required provision computed; the adjusting movement posted with its one-line explanation; specific judgments documented. Write-off candidates are surfaced to their approval path — the ritual nominates; the governance decides. Never both in the same sitting.

5. The statement run. Customer statements out; last month's returned queries confirmed worked; disputes verified on-record.

6. Supplier statement reconciliations. The month's tranche — top suppliers monthly, the rest on rotation. Remainders worked; missed credit notes captured; missing bills chased.

7. The outputs handed upward. The ritual's products go to the close (module 7 receives them): the aged AR and AP with provision netting shown, the advance schedules, the tie confirmation, the write-off log, the unallocated residual. Each a one-page artifact — and each already true, because the ritual made it so.

The economics. Ninety minutes monthly is the compounding investment: skipped for a quarter, every list doubles and the archaeology begins; kept, the year-end AR/AP work is a formality and the audit's receivables programme meets a record with the four adjectives pre-answered. The trading desks receive the ritual's feedback — the unallocated causes, the recurring deduction patterns — rather than attending the sitting.

Practical rule: the ritual has one owner — the accountant, or the credit controller wearing the accounts hat — and a fixed slot in the month. A ritual with a name and a date happens; one without either is a good intention.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's year in the chair
lessons.html:
The accounts chair, installed and lived. Every chapter appears.

The sweep instituted (Chapter 2). Month one's first unallocated read is the expected archaeology: ₦840,000 unallocated across 23 items — payments-on-account going back nine months, four credit notes issued and never applied, two advances whose trades completed unmatched. Three afternoons of matching (customers called with the professional question — your payment of March 14th, against which invoices? — every call also quietly announcing the watched account), one genuine overpayment refunded properly, one escalation: a ₦60,000 payment no record explains, parked named, resolved in week three as a sister-company transfer mis-referenced. The read closes month two at ₦45,000, month three at near-zero — and the aging report, purged of hidden credits, promptly reveals two genuinely overdue accounts the old net balances had camouflaged. The sweep's first commercial dividend, handed to collections.

The provision policy built (Chapter 4). The matrix is built from the business's own history — the last two years' collection outcomes by age band: nil to 60 days, 10% at 61-120, 30% at 121-180, 60% at 181-365, full past a year — written on the policy page and applied to the opening aging. The opening provision: ₦410,000, charged with its explanation to the MD: this is what the aging says the book is worth; the number was always true — now it is booked. Monthly movements thereafter are small and explained, and Q3's release (collections improved) reads as exactly the good news it is, because the policy is stable enough for movements to mean something.

A write-off done right — and the surprise (Chapter 4). Month five: the definitively-gone customer — premises vacated, phones dead, chase dossier complete — ₦188,000 written off on the two-signature path, evidence filed, tax notes captured, the party record retained with its history. Month eleven: the surprise — the customer's principal resurfaces, restarts smaller, and pays ₦120,000 against the old debt for the relationship's sake. The recovery lands as income through the payment machinery, referenced end to end, and the party's history reads whole: debt, chase, write-off, recovery, new terms (cash-and-carry). The accountant's remark: the record survived the write-off, so the recovery had somewhere to land.

The mirror's catch (Chapter 5). The first supplier-statement reconciliation of the top five finds a missing bill — an invoice the supplier shows that never reached the books — captured before it arrived as a surprise demand, and a credit note from a returns batch that was never claimed: ₦74,000 recovered by asking. The monthly tranche joins the ritual.

The ritual settles (Chapter 7). By month six the sitting runs at its promised ninety minutes: tie checked in two, the sweep short, advances aged, the matrix movement one line, statements out, the mirror's tranche done, seven one-page outputs to the close. The MD's year note: the receivables number used to be an opinion. Now it is four answered questions.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the fourth law
lessons.html:
The chair's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the diverged tie. Symptom: the control disagrees with the party sum; nobody knows since when; reports drawn from whichever number suits. Cause: the tie never checked (Chapters 1, 7) — journals to controls, blob migrations, deletions, each divergence compounding undated. Fix: the incident treatment — the journal filter, the divergence dated by working backwards, the correction by the rules, and the monthly check that makes the next divergence a one-month problem instead of a three-year one.

Pattern 2 — the netting sin. Symptom: receivables that shrink when advances arrive; statements customers dispute on sight; a balance sheet position nobody can decompose. Cause: the two directions crushed together (Chapter 3). Fix: advances captured and reported as what they are; the un-netting migration where the sin is historical; and the reader's test — can a banker see the real position from the face of the statement?

Pattern 3 — the perpetual gross. Symptom: receivables at face value for years; aged debts immortal; the write-off unknown as an instrument. Cause: the honesty doctrine absent (Chapter 4) — collectability asserted, never assessed. Fix: the matrix built from the business's own history, the opening provision charged with its adult explanation, and the write-off path governed and used.

Pattern 4 — the silent ledger. Symptom: statements never sent; confirmations dreaded; supplier statements filed unread; disputes living in inboxes. Cause: the record hiding from examination (Chapter 5) — always a symptom of the hygiene it would fail. Fix: the hygiene first (Chapters 2-4), then the routines switched on in order — statements, supplier reconciliations, then the confirmation posture.

Pattern 5 — the immortal advance. Symptom: advances aging past every plausible delivery; the schedule nobody reviews; the supplier advance paid twice. Cause: advances anchored to no expected date, reviewed on no rhythm (Chapter 3). Fix: expected dates at capture, the monthly aging in the ritual, the resolution paths actually walked, and the payment run's open-advance check made structural.

Pattern 6 — the deleted debtor. Symptom: customers who vanish from the ledger with their balances; a record that cannot answer for its own past. Cause: deletion used where the write-off doctrine belonged — completeness broken. Fix: the write-off as the only exit for a debt, the record retained always, and the completeness question standing in every review.

The review list. Confirm you can state: the chair's distinction and the four questions; the unallocated read's three resolutions and why near-zero compounds; both advance directions, the double-payment defence, and the never-net rule; the two stages of the honesty doctrine, the matrix, and the recovery path; the statement run's three returns and the supplier-statement mirror; the detail-never-blobs loading rule and the migration reconciliation; and the seven-step ninety-minute ritual with its outputs.

The fourth law: the chair keeps the record real, collectable, current and complete. Module 5 turns to the tax custodies and Nigerian compliance.

tax_compliance.title: Accounts 5 — Tax Accounting & Nigerian Compliance
tax_compliance.desc: Tax accounting and Nigerian compliance: the custody idea — tax money held, not owned — across the VAT, WHT and payroll compartments; the Nigerian frame with the 2025 reform's working consequences; the monthly VAT position with its two register bridges; WHT as agent and sufferer with the certificate chase; PAYE and the payroll custodies with the tie chain; the six-step filing routine with the zeroing invariant; the compliance calendar and the tax reserve; and the audit evidence posture.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The silent partner: custody
lessons.html:
The tax accounts have appeared one at a time — output VAT at the invoice, input VAT and WHT at the bill, PAYE at the payroll journal. This module consolidates them into what they jointly are: the state's wallet inside the business's chart — and the discipline of a business that holds another party's money professionally.

The custody idea, stated once for everything. Tax money in a trading business is overwhelmingly money the business holds, not money it owes from its own pocket:

• The VAT charged on every invoice was collected from customers for the state.
• The WHT deducted from a supplier's payment is the supplier's tax, held in transit.
• PAYE is the employees' income tax, withheld at source.

The grammar makes it visible — these are all credits to liability accounts (module 1's ₦7,500 VAT line) — and the operational consequence is the module's spine: custody money is not revenue, not cash flow, and not available. A business that treats its VAT account as working capital is spending someone else's money, and remittance day arrives as a crisis exactly as often as that habit holds. Chapter 7's reserve discipline is the cure; this chapter's job is that the disease is understood as what it is.

The wallet's compartments. The custody and near-custody accounts a trading business carries:

• VAT Payable (the output custody) and Input VAT (the claimable asset that offsets it) — Chapter 3 joins them.
• WHT Payable (custody as deducting agent) and WHT Receivable (the mirror — the business's own tax prepaid through customers' deductions, an asset with a chase attached) — Chapter 4.
• The payroll custodies — PAYE, pension, and the statutory family — Chapter 5.
• Beside them, the business's own tax liabilities proper — companies income tax and its kin, provision-style accounts the accountant owns. Distinguished exactly because they are the business's own cost, not custody.

Every compartment is an account (module 1's types), fed by documents and templates (the posting map), reconciled to a register, and cleared by a remittance routine. One pattern, five appearances — which is why one module can hold them all.

Compliance as rhythm, not emergency. Nigerian tax compliance for a documented trading business is a calendar: monthly returns and remittances on fixed days, annual filings on fixed horizons, each obligation with an owner and an evidence file. The module builds toward that boredom deliberately — a compliance function that is boring is a compliance function that is working. Chapters 2-5 cover the taxes; Chapters 6-8 the routine, the calendar, and the audit posture; Chapters 9-10 the case and the review.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Nigerian frame
lessons.html:
The machinery is universal; the landscape is Nigerian. This chapter is the map at working altitude: which taxes touch a trading business, who collects them, and what the 2025 reform reshaped. It is deliberately conceptual — current rates and thresholds are the accountant's living knowledge, not a manual's frozen table.

The taxes that touch a trading business.

• VAT — the consumption tax on supplies, collected and remitted monthly (Chapter 3).
• WHT — the withholding mechanism riding specified payment types, in both directions (Chapter 4).
• PAYE — employees' income tax, withheld monthly and remitted to the state authority of each employee's residence. This is the federal/state split worth memorising early: VAT and companies income tax run federal; PAYE runs to states — one business, several authorities, one calendar.
• Companies Income Tax (CIT) — the business's own annual tax on profits, provisioned through the year; the accountant's core territory.
• The statutory family around payroll — pension, housing, insurance, and training levies (Chapter 5).

Each has its authority, its rhythm, and its account — and the working skill is knowing which machinery serves each, with the computation itself belonging to the accountant and the current statute.

The 2025 reform. The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 and its companion acts consolidated a scattered statute book and restructured administration. The working consequences to hold:

1. The authority landscape was reorganised — the federal service restructured under new legislation, with registrations and filing rails updated accordingly.
2. Thresholds and reliefs were reshaped — small-company regimes, rate structures, and exemption bands moved. The accountant re-reads eligibility annually; the system's contribution is that it can apply whatever the current answer is: templates adjustable, categories flaggable.
3. The compliance infrastructure moved further digital — e-filing as the norm, e-invoicing and fiscalisation advancing. The consequence that matters most for this module: the invoice register and the filed return increasingly reconcile automatically on the authority's side. Register-to-account discipline has moved from good practice to survival — a business whose returns restate its ledger matches by construction; one that files parallel computations gets the mismatch letters.

The competence boundary. This module teaches the machinery: the accounts, the registers, the routines, the evidence. Tax positions — what qualifies, what rate applies, what relief is claimable — belong to the accountant and the tax adviser. Knowing where that line sits is itself a professional skill, and Chapter 8 shows it at its highest-stakes moment: the audit.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — VAT: both sides, one position
lessons.html:
Output and input, joined into the monthly VAT position, and the routine that files it.

The two sides in one breath. Output: every taxable sale charges VAT through the template — CR VAT Payable, the custody growing with trade, the invoice register its document-level mirror. Input: VAT paid on qualifying purchases — DR Input VAT, an asset, the claim's evidence being the supplier's proper invoice. That evidence rule is why invoice quality is a money issue: a ₦100 price with claimable input beats a ₦99 price without it. The chart carries both compartments; the documents feed both automatically; the monthly work is joining them.

The net position. The month's arithmetic: output charged − allowable input = the position.

• Payable when output exceeds input — the normal trading month: remit the net.
• Carry-forward credit when input exceeds output — the heavy-buying month, the import-stocking quarter: the credit rides to offset future output. Refund mechanics exist in principle; carry-forward is the practical road.

The system computes the position because the documents fed it; the return states it; and the reconciliation before filing is the routine's heart: the invoice register's output total ties to the VAT Payable account's movement, and the purchase register's input total ties to the Input VAT account's movement. Two register-to-account bridges, run as one pre-filing checklist line — because a return filed from numbers the ledger cannot reproduce is Chapter 10's pattern wearing a stamp.

The classification edges. Where VAT literacy earns its keep — the categories the templates must express:

• Standard-rated — the default trading reality.
• Zero-rated — taxable at zero. The distinction matters because zero-rated supplies still belong in the return and preserve input claims on their costs.
• Exempt — outside the charge, with the subtle consequence the accountant will care about: input VAT attributable to exempt supplies is generally not claimable.

A mixed-supply business — the pharmacy whose basic-medicine lines ride an exemption while its cosmetics shelf is standard-rated — therefore needs its items tax-categorised correctly at the master level, so the registers can tell the streams apart and the accountant can run the apportionment with clean data. Get the item masters right once, and the classification takes care of itself at every sale; get them wrong, and every return inherits the error.

Practical rules. The pre-filing sequence is fixed: close both registers, tie both bridges to the kobo, prepare the return from the system, and only then file. And the carry-forward months are stated plainly on the position — a credit month is normal trading arithmetic, not a problem to disguise.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — WHT both directions: agent and sufferer
lessons.html:
Withholding tax runs in both directions at once, and each direction has a different accounting life. This is the mechanism businesses most often hold wrong.

As agent: deducting from suppliers. Qualifying payments — services, rent, professional fees, contracts; the types are set by law, the current rates are the accountant's living table — are settled net, with the deduction credited to WHT Payable: the supplier's tax, held. The worked shape: the ₦1,000,000 professional invoice settles as ₦950,000 cash plus ₦50,000 custody. The agent's obligations complete the picture:

1. The custody is remitted monthly by the calendar, the account zeroing after (Chapter 6).
2. The certificates are procured and delivered to the suppliers whose money was withheld — the certificate is the supplier's evidence for their tax credit. An agent who deducts but never delivers certificates quietly injures every supplier it pays, while accumulating its own administrative debt.
3. The deduction-detail register — who, what, when, how much — serves as both the remittance schedule's source and the certificate run's checklist. One register, two jobs.

As sufferer: customers deducting from you. The mirror, and the direction businesses neglect at real cost. Corporate and government customers deduct WHT from their payments — the ₦1,000,000 receivable settling as ₦950,000 cash plus a ₦50,000 deduction. The accounting: the deduction is not a discount, a loss, or a mystery short-payment — it is the business's own income tax, prepaid: DR WHT Receivable (an asset) in the settlement entry, with the customer's certificate as the asset's evidence. Two disciplines make the asset real:

• Capture — every deduction recognised as WHT at allocation: the short-payment coded correctly, the asset built transaction by transaction.
• The certificate chase — the standing worklist: deductions taken, certificates outstanding, aged per customer, chased with the same professionalism as any receivable. An uncertificated deduction is money in limbo: suffered but unprovable.

The asset's destiny. WHT suffered offsets the business's income tax liability — the credit the accountant applies at filing. A business that captures and certificates its deductions pays its CIT net of what it already paid through customers; one that doesn't pays its own tax twice, quietly, year after year. Chapter 9 prices this at HealthTrade: the certificate chase is the module's most reliably self-funding routine.

Summary. Agent side: deduct, remit monthly, deliver certificates, keep the detail register. Sufferer side: capture every deduction as the prepaid asset, chase the certificates as an aged worklist, and hand the credits to the accountant at filing.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — PAYE and the payroll custodies
lessons.html:
The payroll journal credited a row of custody accounts in one line; this chapter opens the row — the employee-money custodies, their rhythms, and the tie that keeps payroll defensible.

The custody family. The monthly payroll carves an employee's gross into destinations, and each destination is an account with an authority behind it:

• PAYE — the employee's income tax, withheld under the current law's bands and reliefs (the 2025 reform reshaped the bands and the low-income threshold — the accountant's living table; the system's contribution is a payroll setup that applies whatever the current structure is). Remitted monthly to the state of each employee's residence: a Lagos head office with Ogun-resident staff files in both states, so the payroll register must split by state to serve it.
• Pension — the contributory scheme's employee and employer portions, remitted to each employee's chosen fund administrator. Plural administrators, one schedule: the register splits by PFA.
• The levy family — housing fund, insurance trust, industrial training — applicability confirmed by the accountant against headcount and sector, each a small account with its own rhythm.

The distinction the grammar makes automatic, held explicitly: withheld-from-employee is custody; borne-by-employer is cost. The employer's own pension share and the levies the business bears are expense, not custody.

The payroll tie. The register-to-account bridge, payroll edition: the payroll register's column totals (gross, PAYE, pension by portion, net pay) tie to the payroll journal's lines, which tie to the custody accounts' movements, which zero at remittance. One chain, checked monthly in minutes — and the chain's health is what makes every payroll question answerable: the employee disputing a deduction (the register's row, the payslip's mirror), the authority querying a remittance (the schedule, the receipt), the auditor sampling a month (the chain, walked end to end).

The payslip. Every employee receives the statement of their own carving — gross, deductions itemised, net — every month. The payslip is the employee's certificate (the WHT logic, personal edition) and the business's first defence in any deduction dispute. It is not optional and not annual.

The rhythms. Monthly: PAYE to each relevant state by its day; pension within days of paying salaries — the tightest window in the family, statutorily pinned to the payment of wages rather than the month's end. Annually: the employer's PAYE returns in the new year's first month, reduced to an extract when the register lived in the system all year — and an archaeology project when it lived in a spreadsheet beside it (Chapter 10's pattern).

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The filing and remittance routine: the zeroing invariant
lessons.html:
Every custody chapter ended at the same machinery. Here it is once, generalised: the monthly routine that turns tax from anxiety into procedure, and the invariant that proves each cycle clean.

The six steps, for any custody.

1. Close the register — the month's document-level detail (invoices for VAT, deductions for WHT, the payroll register for PAYE), cut off at the period. The register is the return's evidence and the account's mirror.
2. Reconcile register to account — the bridge, to the kobo, divergences worked now. A register-account disagreement found before filing is a bookkeeping task; found after, it is an amended return, an authority conversation, or both.
3. Prepare the return from the system — the return restates the ledger. The parallel spreadsheet computation is the pattern this module keeps convicting: two computations guarantee a divergence, and the filed one wins the argument with the authority while the booked one wins it with the auditor. One source, or two problems.
4. File by the date — the calendar's line (Chapter 7), owned by name.
5. Remit — the payment entry, from the reserve (Chapter 7), referenced to the filing.
6. Verify the zero — the invariant, below.

The zeroing invariant. After a clean cycle, each custody account returns to its explainable level — zero for the fully-remitted custodies, the stated carry-forward for VAT credit months. Any unexplained residue is next month's first investigation, because a custody account that will not zero is telling one of a short list of stories:

• A register-account divergence — the bridge skipped.
• A remittance short or misposted — the payment against the wrong account.
• A prior month's residue compounding — the drift that becomes archaeology.
• Custody spent — Chapter 1's disease, surfacing as arithmetic.

The invariant is the routine's self-test: it costs one glance and it catches all four.

The evidence file. Each cycle files its bundle: the register extract, the reconciliation, the return as filed, the filing acknowledgment, the remittance evidence, the zero-verification. One folder per tax per month — boring and complete. This is Chapter 8's audit posture being built monthly as a by-product: the routine that runs well is the routine that evidences well. Its absence is why authority queries paralyse unprepared businesses — the answer exists, but assembling it takes a week, and a week's silence reads as evasion.

Practical rule: the six steps run in order, per custody, on the calendar's days. Steps 2 and 6 — the bridge and the zero — are the two that keep the rest honest, and they are the two that businesses under pressure skip first.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The compliance calendar and the reserve
lessons.html:
The routines need their when and their money. The consolidated calendar, and the reserve discipline that makes remittance day a transfer instead of a crisis.

The calendar. The monthly spine — the specific statutory days are the accountant's confirmation; the shape is universal:

• VAT — return and remittance in the month's third week, for the prior month.
• WHT — remittance on its earlier track; the agent's custody moves faster, with state-collected streams on their own days.
• PAYE — to each relevant state by its mid-month day.
• Pension — within days of paying salaries: the tightest window in the family, pinned to the wage payment itself.

The annual layer rides above: CIT filing on the business's filing horizon months after year-end; the annual PAYE employer returns in the new year's first month; the levy family's annual cycles. The calendar is built once per business — every obligation, its authority, its day, its owner by name, its evidence-file location — and it lives on the policy page, reviewed annually and at every legal change.

The reserve discipline. Chapter 1 named the disease (custody spent); here is the structural cure: the tax custodies segregated in cash, not just in accounts. A tax-reserve bank account — module 3's purpose-per-account rule, now with its most important tenant — receives, on a rhythm, the cash matching the custody balances:

• The month's VAT position swept as it accrues, or at close.
• WHT deductions moved when withheld.
• The payroll custodies parked at the payroll run.

The mechanics are one contra entry per sweep. The discipline is the rule: the reserve is not working capital — it is the state's money sitting in a room with the state's name on it. The payoff is the module's promised boredom: remittance day is a transfer from a funded account, executed by the calendar, with no scramble, no bridging loan, and no conversation about which supplier waits so the state can be paid.

The sizing honesty. Businesses under genuine cash strain resist the sweep — we need that float. The answer is honest, not soft: the custody money was never available, so the strain is real and must be solved with the real tools — collections acceleration, stock discipline, supplier terms, and if necessary actual credit at actual credit prices. Penalties and interest on unremitted custody are the most expensive credit line in Nigeria, taken by default. Chapter 9 shows this exact conversation at HealthTrade, and the alternative that worked.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Audits and the evidence posture
lessons.html:
Sooner or later the authority asks questions — the desk review, the query letter, the field audit. The preparation is not lawyering; it is a posture, built monthly.

The posture in one sentence. Registers tied to accounts tied to documents, filed on time, evidenced in folders. When that chain exists, every authority question is an extraction exercise; when it doesn't, every question is a reconstruction project — and reconstruction under deadline is where businesses concede assessments they never owed. The posture is Chapter 6's evidence file compounding: twelve monthly folders per tax per year, each self-contained, and the audit-support task collapsing to which months, which taxes — here.

The encounter types.

• The desk review — the authority's routine reconciliation of your filings against their expectations, increasingly automated as the e-invoicing rails mature (Chapter 2's point: they now run half the reconciliation themselves). The business whose register fed its returns matches by construction; the mismatch letters go to the businesses that filed parallel computations.
• The query letter — specific questions on specific periods. Answered on record: the reply in writing, the evidence attached, the file noting what was sent and when. Within the stated window, factually, and without volunteering adjacent essays — answer what was asked, completely; the accountant reviews before it goes.
• The field audit — the authority in the building. Preparation is the standing posture plus logistics: a room, and a liaison — one person through whom all requests flow, so the audit gets consistent, logged responses instead of hallway answers. The role division is precise: the system's job is to produce evidence, not arguments — records extracted cleanly, drill-downs demonstrated where they help — while positions are argued by the accountant and the tax adviser.

The common findings, pre-empted. What trading-business audits actually find, each one a chapter of this track running in reverse: output VAT on invoices absent from returns (the register-return divergence — the bridge skipped); input VAT claimed on defective invoices (the evidence rule ignored); WHT deducted but remitted late or not at all (custody spent); PAYE state splits improvised (the register that couldn't split); and payroll journals that tie to no register at all. A business that runs Chapters 3-7 has pre-empted the list — which is the point of running them.

Summary. Build the folders monthly; answer queries on record and within the window; route field audits through one liaison; produce evidence and leave positions to the professionals. A clean posture converts the audit from a threat into an appointment.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Case study: HealthTrade's compliance year
lessons.html:
The silent partner, professionally held. Every chapter appears.

The consolidation (Chapters 1, 3). The first month assembles what the earlier modules built: the four custody accounts confirmed and typed; the item masters' tax categories audited — the pharmacy's exempt basic-medicine lines against its standard-rated cosmetics, 14 items re-categorised, the mixed-supply registers now able to tell their streams apart, and the apportionment question handed to the accountant with clean data. Then the first full monthly VAT routine, end to end: registers closed, both bridges tied to the kobo, the return prepared from the system, filed, remitted from the new reserve, VAT Payable verified at zero. The accountant's note in the file: first month the return and the ledger were the same document.

The certificate chase (Chapter 4). The WHT Receivable archaeology: the sufferer-side register, reconstructed from allocation history, finds ₦1.34m of deductions suffered over two years — certificates held for only ₦610k. The chase is instituted: outstanding certificates listed per customer, aged, worked like receivables — the corporate customers' finance teams contacted with the professional ask; the government customer escalated through its due process. Eight months later, certificates for a further ₦590k are recovered and handed to the accountant for the CIT credit: the business's own tax, un-paid-twice, at the cost of a standing worklist. The remaining ₦140k — deductions by two defunct customers, certificates unobtainable — is written to the accountant's judgment with its file: even the loss is a documented decision instead of a quiet leak.

The reserve's first test (Chapter 7). Month four: a heavy import quarter squeezes cash, and the old instinct surfaces in a management meeting — the VAT account has ₦2.1m sitting idle; borrow it for the Emzor payment, replace it by the 21st. The custody argument is restated — the most expensive credit line in Nigeria, taken by default — and the alternative is worked instead: the receivables push accelerates two collections, and the stock ladder releases a slow line. The reserve stays whole; remittance day passes as a transfer, as designed. The MD's conversion is complete by Q3, when the reserve sweep becomes the month's first standing transfer rather than its last argument.

The desk query (Chapter 8). Month nine brings the authority's automated mismatch letter — for the pre-system period, where a parallel spreadsheet had filed what the old records could not reproduce. The reply is built the on-record way: the current months demonstrated (register, return, remittance, zero — one folder handed over per month), the legacy divergence quantified and explained, the accountant leading the position. The query closes with a small legacy settlement and a sentence in the closing letter that files itself as the module's testimonial: current periods reconcile to source.

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Common mistakes & the fifth law
lessons.html:
The tax layer's recurring failures — each one a business somewhere is living right now — then the review list.

Pattern 1 — custody spent. Symptom: remittance day as recurring crisis; the VAT account funded by scramble; interest and penalties as line items. Cause: the state's money used as float (Chapters 1, 7) — the most expensive credit line in Nigeria, taken by default. Fix: the reserve account with its sweep rhythm, the working-capital problem solved honestly with the real tools, and the custody framing taught until it holds.

Pattern 2 — the parallel computation. Symptom: returns prepared in spreadsheets beside the system; filed numbers and booked numbers diverging; nobody able to say which is true. Cause: two sources (Chapter 6) — the return no longer restates the ledger. Fix: the return from the system, the register bridges as the pre-filing gate, and the spreadsheet retired to what it should be — a formatting tool, never a source.

Pattern 3 — the unreconciled registers. Symptom: register totals and account movements drifting apart unexamined; the desk review's mismatch letter arriving as a surprise. Cause: the bridges skipped (Chapters 3, 6) — while the authority's e-invoice rails now run their half automatically. Fix: the register-to-account line in every monthly routine, divergences worked before filing, and the zeroing invariant verified as each cycle's close.

Pattern 4 — certificates uncollected. Symptom: WHT suffered for years with a certificate file that fits in an envelope; the CIT bill paid gross. Cause: the sufferer side run on resignation (Chapter 4) — the business's own tax paid twice, quietly. Fix: the deduction captured at allocation, the chase as a standing aged worklist, and the recovered credits handed to the accountant with their evidence — the module's most reliably self-funding routine.

Pattern 5 — payroll beside the system. Symptom: salaries in a spreadsheet, a monthly lump journal, PAYE computed elsewhere, state splits improvised, the annual return an archaeology project. Cause: the register that can produce any slice replaced by one that produces none (Chapter 5). Fix: payroll into the system (or rigorously bridged), the custody chain checked monthly, payslips as the standing employee certificate, and the annual return reduced to an extract.

Pattern 6 — penalties as a cost of doing business. Symptom: late-filing and late-remittance penalties absorbed without comment, month after month. Cause: no calendar, no owners, no reserve — the whole module absent. Fix: the calendar built with named owners, the reserve funded, and the penalty line watched to zero: it is the single clearest gauge of whether this module is installed.

The review list. Confirm you can state: the custody idea and the wallet's compartments; the Nigerian tax set with the federal/state split and the 2025 reform's three working consequences; the VAT net position, the two bridges, and the three classifications with the mixed-supply rule; both WHT directions with the ₦1m worked shape, the certificate obligations, and the chase; the payroll custody family, the tie chain, and the payslip rule; the six-step routine and the zeroing invariant's four stories; the calendar's shape and the reserve discipline; and the audit posture with its three encounter types.

The fifth law: tax money is held, not owned — reconciled to its registers, filed from the system, remitted from the reserve, and zeroed every cycle. Module 6 turns to the address system: cost centers and dimensions.
