dimensions.title: Accounts 6 — Cost Centers & Dimensions
dimensions.desc: Cost centers and dimensions: one chart, many lenses — the cost center tree designed from the accountability structure, the default cascade and mandatory validation that address every posting, the branch P&L read as contribution before fully-loaded with the close-on-contribution rule, the allocation rules (direct first; written, stable, visible bases), budgets per address with cause-before-comment variance reads, and the second dimension's earning test for service lines and projects.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Profit has an address
lessons.html:
Module 1 planted the rule in one sentence — the chart answers what kind of money; dimensions answer whose and where — and deferred the machinery here. This module is that machinery: how one business reads many profits — per branch, per service line, per project — without the chart ever learning their names.

The question this module answers. Every owner of a multi-branch business asks it, usually in the first meeting: which branch actually makes money? The unstructured answer is folklore — the flagship "carries" the network, the new branch "must be losing", the service side "pays for itself" — all asserted, none known. The structured answer requires that every naira of revenue and cost carries, from the moment it posts, an address: the branch, the line, the project it belongs to. Then the P&L can be filtered by address and read true. That address is the dimension, and the module's design rule governs everything in it: one chart, many lenses — the chart stays a single language (Rent is one account, everywhere), and the dimensions multiply the readings of it (Rent at Ibadan, Rent at Akure) without multiplying the words.

The disease this module prevents. The alternative design, met constantly: the per-branch chart copy — Rent - Ibadan, Rent - Akure, Rent - HQ, and so on for every expense and every branch. Three branches turn a 60-line P&L structure into 180 accounts; five branches into 300. Every new branch becomes chart surgery, every firm-wide read a manual re-addition of scattered leaves, and every posting a navigation exercise through near-identical names, with the mis-post rate rising with the count. The cure: the branch belongs in the dimension field, entered once, cascading by default (Chapter 3), and the chart never grows when the business does. The test of the design is exactly that: opening branch four should touch the dimension list and not one account.

What dimensions are not. Three boundary stakes before the machinery:

• Not a second chart. Dimensions carry no balances of their own — they are tags on GL entries, and every dimensional read is the same GL, filtered.
• Not only for the P&L — balance-sheet dimensioning exists and has uses — but the P&L is where the payoff lives and where this module works.
• Not free. Every mandatory dimension taxes every posting forever, which is why Chapter 7 guards the door on adding more.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the cost center tree. Chapter 3: the wiring — defaults, cascade, validation. Chapter 4: the branch P&L and how to read it honestly. Chapter 5: allocating shared costs. Chapter 6: budgets against actuals. Chapter 7: the second dimension — service lines and projects. Chapter 8: HealthTrade's addresses. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Cost centers: the address book
lessons.html:
The primary dimension has a name and a structure: the cost center — and its design follows the same tree rules as the warehouse tree and the chart.

The tree. Cost centers form a tree: group cost centers for rollup reading (Branches; Operations), and leaf cost centers that take postings (Ibadan Branch; Akure Branch; Head Office). Postings to groups are refused by design — the third appearance of the rule: money exists at leaves; groups exist so leaves can be read together. The company's tree roots at a main cost center that anchors the whole. Every earlier tree discipline transfers untouched: named for the decade, shallow (two levels below root serves almost every trading business), designed from what must be read, changed as governed events, retired rather than deleted.

Designing the address book. The design question is whose performance the business manages — the accountability structure, not the org chart's vanity:

• A leaf per unit that has an owner and a monthly P&L conversation: each branch (a manager answers for it); head office (the shared-function home Chapter 5 allocates from); the warehouse or distribution operation where it is managed as its own unit.
• Not a leaf per paper department, per team of two, or per activity nobody reviews separately. The reading test again: a cost center that nobody's monthly conversation names is sprawl wearing a lanyard.

A shortcut that makes design fast: the cost center tree usually shadows the warehouse tree's accountability layer — the people who answer for stock are frequently the people who answer for the P&L. Where the two trees diverge, the divergence should be explainable in one sentence, or it is a mistake in one tree or the other.

The default machinery. Three layers carry the addressing labour:

1. The company default — the unaddressed posting's fallback. Chapter 3 argues this fallback should almost never fire.
2. Master defaults — the warehouse or branch record wired to its cost center; item groups where product-line reading matters; and…
3. User defaults — where the operator is the address: the till assistant whose every posting belongs to their branch.

The design goal: a well-wired business addresses ninety-something percent of its postings without anyone touching the field. The address is written by the setup, not by discipline — because discipline decays and defaults don't.

Practical rule: keep the leaf count honest. Each leaf is a monthly page someone must own and read; a tree with more leaves than owners is already telling you which ones to merge.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Wiring the address into every posting
lessons.html:
An address book is useless if letters go unaddressed. This chapter is the wiring: where the dimension gets written, how defaults cascade, and the validation that makes the address a rule instead of a hope.

Where the address is written. Every P&L-touching document carries the field, at two levels:

• Header level — the whole document one address: the branch invoice, the branch expense.
• Row level — each line its own address: the head-office purchase that splits across branches, the invoice mixing service lines. Row overrides header, because real documents mix addresses more often than design imagines.

The posting map (module 1) gains its dimension column: the sales invoice's income line carries the selling branch (cascaded from the till, the warehouse, or the user); the delivery's COGS carries the same (the warehouse-to-cost-center wiring doing the work); the purchase invoice's expense lines carry their consumers (row-level where consumption splits); the journal's rows carry theirs (module 2 already demanded it — an expense journal that charges without addressing is a letter posted blank); and payroll carries each employee's unit.

The cascade. Defaults resolve in a fixed order — the specific beats the general:

1. The row's explicit entry, over
2. The header's, over
3. The master-derived default (item group, warehouse, customer where wired), over
4. The user's default, over
5. The company fallback.

The wiring hour sets this cascade so the front line almost never sees the field: the Ibadan till user's sales land at Ibadan because the user and the warehouse both say so; the Akure expense claim lands at Akure because the claimant does. The field surfaces for human decision only where the machine genuinely cannot know — the shared purchase, the split service — which is exactly where a human should decide.

Validation: the address as a rule. The dimension-validation settings close the gap between mostly-addressed and always-addressed: dimensions marked mandatory for the account ranges that need them — all income and expense accounts, at minimum — so the P&L posting that cannot save without its address never posts blank. The company fallback then catches only what validation deliberately exempts, and the monthly test is simple: the unaddressed lump at the default cost center should be at or near zero. A growing lump means a gap in the cascade or an exemption that should not exist — swept to true addresses while small, and the gap fixed at its source.

Practical rule: verify the wiring the same way the posting map was verified — one live document per kind, the addresses read aloud. An hour at setup buys a P&L that filters true from month one.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The branch P&L: the payoff read
lessons.html:
The addresses exist so this page can: the branch P&L — the owner's first-meeting question, answered monthly and honestly. The read has two halves, and keeping them separate is the chapter's whole discipline.

The natural half: revenue and direct cost. Filtered by the branch's cost center, the P&L's top assembles itself from the wiring: revenue by branch (every sale carried its source), COGS by branch (the delivery's valuation release carried it too), and the branch's direct expenses — its rent, its payroll, its power, its local running costs, each posted with its address at entry. This much is arithmetic, and its honesty is exactly the wiring's honesty — which is why the unaddressed-lump sweep precedes every monthly read.

The harder half: shared costs. Head office exists — the MD's salary, the accountant, the shared warehouse, group marketing, the system's own subscription — and none of it posted to a branch, because none of it belongs to one. Should it appear on branch P&Ls at all? Chapter 5 holds the allocation rules; this chapter holds the reading frame that makes them usable: contribution before net.

• The contribution view — branch revenue minus branch COGS minus branch direct costs — answers the operational question: does this branch, as a trading unit, generate surplus? Every number on the page is a fact: posted where it happened, nothing estimated, nothing arguable. This is the branch manager's page — they control everything on it.
• The fully-loaded view — contribution minus an allocated share of head office — answers a different question: does the branch cover its share of existing overheads? Its numbers are part fact, part policy (the allocation basis is a choice). This is the owner's portfolio page — worth seeing, dangerous to act on alone.

Keep the two views separate and labelled, always.

The classic misread, pre-empted. The fully-loaded view's danger closes branches that should stay open. The newest or smallest branch shows a fully-loaded loss — its allocated overhead share swamps its young contribution — and someone proposes closing it. Walk the arithmetic before agreeing: close the branch and its contribution leaves the network, while the allocated overhead stays and re-lands on the surviving branches. The business is poorer by the contribution, and the loaded view now frowns at the next-smallest branch. The rule that prevents the spiral: open, close, and expand on contribution; use the loaded view only to size the overhead conversation. Chapter 8 shows the rule earning its keep at HealthTrade's Akure branch.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Allocating shared costs
lessons.html:
The costs that genuinely serve everyone must either stay unallocated — honest, but the loaded view stays unbuilt — or be shared by rule. The allocation rules: brief, written, and deliberately boring.

Direct first, always. The first rule shrinks the problem before sharing it: everything attributable at source is posted there and never enters allocation. The group marketing campaign that ran for one branch's opening is that branch's. The head-office staffer seconded to a project is the project's. The shared warehouse's costs, where the warehouse serves branches measurably, can be recharged by throughput if the business wants that precision. Every naira attributed directly is a naira the allocation argument never touches — mature businesses allocate a residue, not a bloc: the smaller the allocated pool, the smaller the fiction, and the quieter the arguments.

Bases for the residue. What remains — genuinely joint costs — shares by a written basis, chosen per cost family:

• Revenue share — the default for general overheads: simple, proportional to activity.
• Headcount — for people-driven costs: HR, welfare, training.
• Space — for premises-driven costs where premises are shared.
• Throughput — for the distribution recharge, where measured.

The specific numbers matter less than three properties. The basis is written — on the policy page, so every allocation question is answered by pointing, not arguing. It is stable — changed annually at most, as an event with a memo; a basis that moves monthly is a dial, and movements should mean something. And it is visible — allocated lines shown as allocated on the loaded view: labelled, separable, never blended into direct costs, so any reader can reconstruct contribution by covering one section with a thumb.

The allocation wars, and their treaty. Where allocation is argued monthly, the pattern is always the same three failures: the basis is unwritten or unstable; the allocated pool is too large (direct-first neglected); and the loaded view is being used for decisions it cannot carry — branch bonuses on loaded profit is the classic accelerant, converting an accounting convention into a monthly salary dispute. The treaty reverses all three: direct-first shrinks the pool, the written basis freezes annually, the lines stay labelled — and incentives move to contribution, the page the manager actually controls.

Practical rule: when an allocation argument starts, do not defend the number — point at the page. If the page cannot settle it, the page is what needs fixing, once, rather than the argument monthly.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Budgets vs actuals: the forward address
lessons.html:
Dimensions address the past; budgets address the future — and the machinery joins them: the budget set per address, the actuals landing beside it, and the monthly variance read that turns the pair into management.

The budget machinery. Budgets attach where the reading lives: per cost center (the branch's expense budget; head office's own), per account or account group, per fiscal year with a monthly or periodic distribution — the even split for steady costs, the seasonal curve for the trade that has one (the December-heavy retail budget expects its own Q4). The system holds the budget beside the actuals it accumulates, and the variance — actual against budget, by address, by account, monthly and cumulative — becomes a standing read instead of a spreadsheet reunion.

Budget actions. Where wanted, the machinery acts on exceeding: warn, or stop. The hard stop is reserved for the account families where overspend is a governance failure rather than a trading reality — a stop on COGS in a good sales month is the machinery fighting the business. Warn widely; stop narrowly.

Building budgets that mean something. Budget quality is structural, not aspirational:

1. Built per address from that address's own history — the branch's last-year actuals as the base, which the address system supplies by construction: the wiring's first forward dividend.
2. Adjusted by known changes — the new branch's ramp, the rent review, the headcount plan.
3. Owned by the address's owner — the branch manager who built their number defends it differently than one who received it; the budget conversation is the accountability structure exercising.
4. Approved as a set — the rollup must reconcile to the business's plan. Branch ambitions summing to more than the network's cash is a conversation for November, not a discovery in March.

The variance read. Monthly, by address, with one discipline: cause before comment. A variance decomposes — volume versus rate (sold more units, or spent more per unit); timing versus level (the cost that moved months, or the cost that grew); one-off versus run-rate (the repair that happened, or the drift that will repeat) — and the read's output is the standard shape: the material variances, each carrying a one-line story and, where needed, an action with an owner. Thresholds keep the read short: variances below the line are noise; the read exists for the stories.

Practical rule: a budget cited only in January and December is decoration, and a budget used mainly for blame teaches managers to pad numbers and hide news. The monthly read, seated in the close, causes before comments, is what keeps the instrument alive.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Projects and service lines: the second dimension
lessons.html:
The cost center answered where; some businesses need a second question answered — what line, which job — and the accounting-dimension machinery carries it. The second lens, and the guard that keeps lenses from multiplying into fog.

When a dimension earns existence. The reading test at its sternest, because every mandatory dimension taxes every posting forever. A second dimension earns its field when all three hold:

1. Someone will read its cut monthly and act on it.
2. The cut crosses the first dimension — the service line that exists at several branches. If it nests inside one branch, the cost center tree already carries it.
3. The postings can be attributed at entry with reasonable defaults — a dimension the front line cannot fill truthfully fills falsely; the address system's honesty is only ever the entry moment's honesty.

Two dimensions serve almost every trading business that needs any; the third is rare and argued hard; the fourth is fog.

The service-line lens. The mixed business's standing need — the pharmacy with a clinic corner, the retailer with an installation arm, the distributor with a logistics-for-hire side: one branch, two businesses, and the branch P&L alone cannot say which one earns. The service-line dimension cuts the same GL the other way: revenue by line (the invoice rows carry it — item-group defaults doing the cascade: clinic services default to Clinic, shop items to Retail), direct costs by line (the clinic's pharmacist, its consumables), and the two-way read the pair of dimensions unlocks — the branch-by-line matrix (Ibadan's clinic against Akure's clinic; each branch's retail core). That matrix answers expansion's real question: not should we add clinics, but the clinic line contributes X at Ibadan and Y at Akure — what differs, and which model travels? Contribution framing governs exactly as in Chapter 4, and shared-within-branch costs (the premises both lines sit in) allocate by Chapter 5's rules or, better, stay at the branch's shared level unallocated.

The project lens. Job-shaped work — the fit-out contract, the installation project, the one-off supply tender — wants revenue, costs, and margin per job. The project dimension carries it, with the one property branches and lines don't have: a lifecycle. Projects open when the job opens and close when it closes — opened with a code and an owner, posted to while live, read at completion (the job's margin against its quote: the estimating feedback loop), and closed so the value list stays short and current. A project list full of ancient open codes is the dimension decaying into noise.

Practical rule: before adding any dimension, write the monthly read it will serve and name its reader. No named reader, no dimension.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's addresses
lessons.html:
The address system, installed and read. Every chapter appears.

The tree and the wiring (Chapters 2-3). The design hour with the MD and the accountant produces four leaves under two groups — Branches (Central/Lagos, Ibadan, Akure) and Head Office — shadowing the warehouse tree's accountability layer exactly. The one divergence gets its one-sentence justification: the shared distribution operation takes its own leaf, because it is managed as a unit and will be read as one. Defaults cascade from warehouses and users; income and expense accounts get mandatory validation; and the posting map is re-verified with its new dimension column — one live document per kind, addresses read aloud. Month one's unaddressed lump: ₦0 — the validation refused every blank at birth.

The first branch P&L, and the MD's lesson (Chapter 4). Month two's read, contribution format, three branches side by side: Central contributes strongly, Ibadan solidly — and Akure, eight months old, contributes ₦310,000… which the fully-loaded view (head office allocated by revenue share) turns into a ₦140,000 "loss". The MD's first instinct is the classic — Akure isn't working — and the arithmetic is walked at the whiteboard: close Akure and its ₦310k contribution leaves the network; the allocated overhead stays and re-lands on Central and Ibadan; the business is ₦310k a month poorer, and the loaded view now frowns at Ibadan. The lesson lands as the rule — close on contribution, expand on contribution — and Akure, read rightly, is a young branch working, not a loss. The loaded view keeps its one real job: it sizes the head-office conversation, which produces one genuine action — the group's software and admin stack is renegotiated, head office lightens 8%, and every branch's loaded view improves without a single allocation argument.

The policy settles an argument (Chapter 5). Month four: the Ibadan manager disputes the marketing allocation — a campaign that only helped Lagos. The policy page answers by pointing: campaign costs attributable to a branch post direct — and this one, on inspection, was indeed Lagos-specific, mis-posted to the shared pool and corrected by the rules to Central's direct costs. The residue keeps sharing by the written basis. The argument dies in one meeting because the page, not the loudest voice, decides.

Budgets arrive (Chapter 6). Year two's budgets are built per branch from each branch's own year-one actuals, adjusted for known changes (Akure's ramp, the Central rent review), owned by the managers who built them, and approved as a reconciling set. The monthly variance read seats itself in the close: causes before comments, thresholds keeping it short — and February's first real story (Ibadan's power spend up 40%: a generator fault, one-off, fixed) is discussed in week one instead of discovered in an argument at year-end.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the sixth law
lessons.html:
The address layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the per-branch chart copy. Symptom: Rent-Ibadan, Rent-Akure, Rent-HQ… hundreds of accounts, chart surgery at every opening, firm-wide reads assembled by hand. Cause: the address written into the language (Chapter 1) — dimensions unknown or distrusted at setup. Fix: the migration — dimensions wired, the copies merged to single accounts by documented entries with history preserved, validation installed, the chart returned to one language. Priced honestly as the archaeology it is.

Pattern 2 — the unaddressed lump. Symptom: a default cost center absorbing a growing share of the P&L; branch reads everyone quietly distrusts. Cause: the optional address decaying (Chapter 3) — blanks accumulating where validation should have refused them. Fix: the lump swept to true addresses while small, mandatory validation on the P&L ranges, the cascade tightened so the field almost never surfaces — and the monthly sweep kept as the standing hygiene line before every branch read.

Pattern 3 — allocation wars. Symptom: monthly arguments about shared-cost shares; bonuses fought over loaded profit; the basis renegotiated by whoever shouts. Cause: the rules absent (Chapter 5) — pool too large, basis unwritten, the loaded view overloaded with decisions it cannot carry. Fix: direct-first shrinking the pool, the written basis frozen annually, labelled and separable lines, and incentives moved to contribution.

Pattern 4 — the death-spiral close. Symptom: the smallest branch closed on its loaded loss; the network poorer; the next branch now "losing". Cause: allocation-led decisions (Chapter 4) — the misread institutionalised. Fix: the arithmetic taught before it is needed, contribution governing open/close/expand calls, and the loaded view returned to its one job: sizing the overhead conversation.

Pattern 5 — budget theatre. Symptom: budgets built in January, cited in December, absent in between; managers budgeting slack and hiding news. Cause: the instrument as decoration, or as punishment (Chapter 6) — either kills the conversation it exists to create. Fix: the monthly variance read seated in the close, thresholds that surface stories rather than noise, causes before comments — and the culture reset: variances are for discussing early, not punishing late.

Pattern 6 — dimension fog. Symptom: four mandatory dimensions; the front line inventing values to save documents; every read doubted. Cause: lenses added without the three-part earning test (Chapter 7). Fix: the test applied retroactively — dimensions nobody reads retired, attribution honesty restored at entry, and the discipline going forward: no named reader, no dimension.

The review list. Confirm you can state: the one-chart-many-lenses rule and the branch-four test; the cost center tree's design rules and the default layers; the cascade order and the mandatory-validation rule with the zero-lump test; contribution versus fully-loaded and the close-on-contribution rule with its arithmetic; the allocation rules — direct first, written stable visible bases, and the treaty; budget quality's four structural properties and cause-before-comment; and the second dimension's three-part earning test with the service-line matrix and the project lifecycle.

The sixth law: one chart, many lenses — every posting carries its address, contribution decides, and allocation is written. Module 7 assembles the period close and the financial statements.

close_statements.title: Accounts 7 — Period Close & Financial Statements
close_statements.desc: The period close and the financial statements: the monthly close with its nine-line checklist and day-five target, cut-off and the completeness pairs, reading the P&L (four rules, pre-reading checks), the balance sheet's line-by-line checks with the equity rule, the cash flow statement's three sections and four-question read, fixed assets and depreciation with the capitalisation policy and annual verification, and year-end as the twelfth close plus annual mechanics.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The period close
lessons.html:
The period close is the monthly procedure that takes a month from trading to sealed. This module covers the close itself, the cut-off discipline at its boundary, the three financial statements produced from a sealed month, the fixed-asset layer the statements require, and the year-end.

Definition. A close is complete when:

1. All the month's documents are in (cut-off — Chapter 3).
2. The recurring manual entries have run and the month's journals have been reviewed (module 2).
3. The standing reconciliations and checks have been performed (Chapter 2 lists them in order).
4. The trial balance has been scanned and its anomalies worked (module 1).
5. The period has been locked — the freeze date advanced so the sealed month cannot change.

A closed month is a month whose statements can be circulated without qualification. Once sealed, its figures stay as reported; corrections discovered later post in the current period under module 2's rules.

Why the close is monthly. The alternative — trading all year and closing once — produces the year-end backlog: twelve months of unposted stragglers, unswept suspense, unreconciled banks, and unaccrued costs, all processed at once, months after the events. The monthly close avoids this by construction:

• Each month's work is small because the previous month's was done.
• Errors are found while their evidence is fresh and the people involved remember the transaction.
• The year-end becomes an ordinary close plus a short list of annual mechanics (Chapter 8).

The cost curve is predictable: a business's first monthly close takes days, because it carries the backlog; by the sixth, the close takes hours. The standing target used in this track is day five — the month sealed and its statements read by the fifth working day of the next month.

The three statements. Produced from the sealed month and read together:

• The profit and loss statement — what the period earned and consumed (Chapter 4).
• The balance sheet — what the business owns and owes at the sealed date (Chapter 5).
• The cash flow statement — where the money went, reconciling profit to bank movement (Chapter 6).

Module contents. Chapter 2: the close checklist. Chapter 3: cut-off. Chapters 4-6: reading the three statements. Chapter 7: fixed assets and depreciation. Chapter 8: year-end, the audit, and the HealthTrade case. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The monthly close checklist
lessons.html:
The close runs from one checklist: nine lines, each with a named owner, run in order. Order matters because later lines verify earlier ones.

1. Cut-off sweep. The month's documents in: unsubmitted drafts found and posted (deliveries picked but unposted, receipts at the gate, invoices pending), straggler paperwork posted with honest in-period dates, and the To-Bill queues read in both directions — the unbilled delivery and the unbilled receipt both distort next month's margin. Chapter 3 covers this line in full.

2. The manual layer. The recurring journal set run (accruals, prepayment consumptions, payroll, depreciation — module 2's templates); accrual reversals verified; the month's journal review performed (the five questions, the count, the aggregate patterns).

3. The sweeps. Suspense to zero, each item classified to its true account. The unaddressed dimension lump to its true cost centers (module 6). Unallocated payments and unapplied credits worked (module 4's read).

4. The reconciliations. Every bank account against its statement (module 3), remainders named and aged. Cash counts confirmed current.

5. The bridges. Stock ledger to stock accounts, to the kobo. Tax registers to tax accounts (module 5's pre-filing check, run whether or not a filing falls this week). Control accounts to party totals (module 4's tie check).

6. Subsidiary outputs collected. The AR/AP ritual's artifacts (aged reports, provision movement, advance schedules), the tax cycles' zero-verifications, the stock month-end's outputs — collected from their own routines, not re-performed here.

7. The trial balance scan. Module 1's ten minutes: wrong-side balances, should-be-zero accounts with balances, unrecognised lines — each flagged and worked.

8. The freeze advance. Stragglers confirmed in, the checks above confirmed passed, then the period locked — accounts and stock together — and the freeze month logged. The order is fixed: sweep first, freeze second. A close that freezes first manufactures its own next-month stragglers.

9. Statements produced and read. The three statements printed from the sealed month; the management reading held (Chapters 4-6); the close bundle filed — the signed checklist plus its artifacts, one folder per month.

Practical rules. The checklist has one owner overall and a named owner per line. Lines 1-8 target days one to four; line 9 lands day five. A line that keeps slipping is investigated as a process problem, not re-assigned as a person problem, until the cause is fixed.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Cut-off
lessons.html:
Cut-off is the rule that a period contains exactly its own documents. Cut-off errors are the close's most common defect and the P&L's most direct distortion: a document in the wrong period moves real margin between months, through omission alone.

The completeness pairs. Cut-off is checked as pairs of documents that must complete within the period:

• Deliveries and their invoices. A period's revenue is its invoices; its COGS is its deliveries. A month whose deliveries posted but whose invoices lagged carries COGS without revenue — margin understated this month, overstated next month when the invoices land. The To-Bill (sales) queue at close is the exposure, in naira: the close either bills it or carries it knowingly, with a note.
• Receipts and their bills. The Stock Received But Not Billed accrual handles this side by design: possession is booked at receipt, and the liability accrues whether or not the supplier's invoice has arrived. The close's job here is the RNB age read: an old RNB balance means invoices are not being processed — a workflow problem, visible as an aging accrual.
• Consumptions and their accruals. Utilities consumed but unbilled, services received but uninvoiced: covered by module 2's accrual routine, run as checklist line 2.

The document sweep, step by step.

1. List draft documents: every document type, filtered unsubmitted, dated this month. This five-minute query finds most of the stragglers.
2. Read the operational queues: the warehouse's unposted receipts, the billing desk's pending list.
3. Anticipate the known latecomers: the supplier who always bills on the 5th for the prior month is accrued by template and reversed on arrival.
4. Run the sweep on day one of the close, so stragglers post with honest in-period dates before the freeze. Sweep first, freeze second.

Worked example. A ₦500,000 delivery posts on the 30th; its invoice posts on the 2nd. Month one records the COGS (say ₦380,000) with no revenue: margin understated by ₦120,000. Month two records ₦500,000 revenue with no COGS: margin overstated by ₦120,000. One document's timing has distorted two months' margins in opposite directions — which is why a gross margin that swings on stable trade points first to cut-off (Chapter 9, Pattern 3).

Summary. Check the pairs: deliveries/invoices via the To-Bill queue, receipts/bills via the RNB age, consumptions via the accrual routine. Sweep on day one, with honest dates, before the freeze.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Reading the profit and loss statement
lessons.html:
The P&L states what the period earned and consumed. This chapter covers its structure, the reading method, and the checks to run before trusting it.

Structure, top to bottom.

• Revenue — the period's invoiced trade, net of returns and credit notes.
• Cost of goods sold — the delivered goods' carried cost: the valuation releases summing.
• Gross margin — the difference, read with its percentage: the trading engine's health in one number, and the first line every reader checks.
• Operating expenses — the running costs, grouped as the chart's design intended them to be read.
• Operating profit — what the business earned before financing and tax.
• Below the line — finance costs; exceptional items, labelled as such (an exceptional item blended into operations distorts every trend); and the tax charge (the business's own tax — module 5's distinction) toward net profit.

The reading method, four rules in order.

1. Trend before level. Read this month against the last six. A level alone says little; a gross margin that moved from 24% to 21% over a quarter is a finding regardless of whether 21% is acceptable in itself.
2. Rate before naira. Margins and expense ratios compare across months of different sizes; raw naira mislead.
3. Decompose before concluding. A falling gross margin splits three ways — price (selling cheaper), mix (selling different things), or cost (paying more) — three different causes with three different owners. Module 6's dimensions do the splitting: margin by branch, by line.
4. Drill before disputing. Every line is three clicks from its documents. The disputed expense is opened live, not argued from the page.

The pre-reading checks. Before the figures are trusted, confirm the disciplines that keep them honest held this month:

• Cut-off (Chapter 3) — the usual cause of a bouncing margin.
• Valuation — a COGS jump caused by a bad rate entering the valuation stream; the rate-history read is the check.
• Accruals (module 2) — the "cheap" month that simply has not been billed yet.
• The dimension lump (module 6) — branch reads distorted by unaddressed postings.
• Exceptional labelling — one-offs marked as one-offs.

The management reading. Twenty minutes, monthly, on a fixed day: the three-number headline (revenue, gross margin percentage, operating profit), the trend view, the material variances with their one-line causes, and any decision the figures require. The reading is a standing meeting, not an email.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Reading the balance sheet
lessons.html:
The balance sheet states what the business owns and owes at the sealed date. The total always balances — the grammar guarantees it — so the reading discipline is line by line: every line is a claim, and every claim has a check.

Structure. Assets: fixed assets (Chapter 7), stock, debtors, prepayments and supplier advances, WHT receivable, bank and cash. Liabilities: creditors, customer advances, accrued expenses, the tax custodies, loans. Equity: capital, retained earnings, the current year's result.

The line-by-line checks.

• Stock — is the figure the perpetual ledger's figure (the stock-to-accounts bridge agreeing), at honest cost, with the dead-stock and aging reads qualifying how good the asset is beyond how big?
• Debtors — gross less the provision, with the provision shown rather than hidden; tied to parties; aged honestly; advances un-netted. The check: does the aging support the provision, and does the tie hold?
• Prepayments and supplier advances — the prepaid rent consuming on schedule; the advance aging clean of items past plausible delivery.
• WHT receivable — certificated, or under active chase; the asset is only as real as its certificate file.
• Bank and cash — every balance reconciled this month, with the reconciliation statements in the close bundle; remainders young and named; floats counted.
• Creditors — tied to parties; the RNB age read; the supplier-statement reconciliations current for the top names.
• Customer advances and accruals — each with its schedule; these liabilities are what keep the P&L honest.
• Tax custodies — at their explainable levels (post-remittance zero, or the stated carry-forward), with the reserve funded to match.
• Equity — retained earnings moves only by the year-end closing entry and governed distributions. An unexplained equity movement is a serious finding (Chapter 9, Pattern 5): deleted documents, forced balances, and migration errors all surface in equity, because equity is the residual where broken books hide.

The reading habit. The balance sheet is read after the P&L in the same monthly sitting: the working-capital lines against last month (stock, debtors, creditors — the movements Chapter 6 restates as cash), the custody levels, and any line whose check failed. A line that cannot answer its check is worked before the statements circulate, or circulated with an explicit note — never silently.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Reading the cash flow statement
lessons.html:
The cash flow statement reconciles two facts that regularly diverge: the P&L reports a profit while the bank balance falls, or the reverse. Most trading businesses never read theirs; this chapter makes it usable.

Why profit and cash differ. Profit records earnings: an invoice raised is revenue whether or not the customer has paid. Cash records movements. The gap between them is the balance sheet moving:

• Profit that became stock — margin sitting in the warehouse as goods.
• Profit that became debtors — margin sitting in unpaid invoices.
• Profit consumed by paying creditors down.
• Profit spent on assets — the cold room is a balance-sheet item, not an expense.

A profitable business can run out of cash, and a cash-rich business can be unprofitable. The cash flow statement starts from profit and shows, movement by movement, where the money went.

The three sections.

1. Operating — the trading engine's cash: profit, adjusted for non-cash lines (depreciation added back — it consumed no cash), and for the working-capital movements (stock up consumes cash; debtors up consumes cash; creditors up releases cash). A healthy trading business generates positive operating cash most months. A profitable business with chronically negative operating cash is growing while burying its margin in stock and debtors faster than it earns it — the figure that explains why growth "doesn't feel like it".
2. Investing — the asset spend: vehicles, fit-outs, equipment (Chapter 7's capitalisations landing as outflows).
3. Financing — the owners' and lenders' money: capital in, loans drawn and repaid, distributions out.

The three sections sum to the month's bank movement, which reconciles to the bank statements — the statement proving itself against module 3's reconciliation.

The five-minute monthly read. The formal statement exists; the working read is four questions:

1. Did operating cash come in positive — did the engine generate or consume?
2. Which working-capital line moved most, and why (one sentence per material movement)?
3. What was invested, and was it planned?
4. What financed the difference — and is that source sustainable?

Practical rule: when the P&L and the bank appear to disagree, do not argue from either — open the cash flow. The disagreement is always one of the working-capital lines, and the statement names which.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Fixed assets and depreciation
lessons.html:
Fixed assets are purchases that outlive their purchase month — vehicles, generators, cold rooms, fit-outs — and depreciation is the mechanism that spreads their cost across their useful lives. This chapter covers the layer at the level the system role requires; the policy choices belong to the accountant.

Capitalise or expense. Every purchase invoice containing a durable item forces the decision:

• Expense — the cost lands in this month's P&L. Correct for consumables and small tools.
• Capitalise — the cost becomes an asset, expensed gradually as depreciation. Correct for durable, material items.

The instrument is the written capitalisation policy: a value threshold (below it, expense regardless — a ₦40,000 printer is not worth an asset record's lifetime of administration), a category list (what the business capitalises, into which asset classes, at which useful lives — the accountant's table), and the rule that the threshold is policy, not discretion. Expensing everything to dampen a good year, or capitalising to flatter a bad one, is the same abuse as moving a provision by mood.

The asset register. Capitalised assets live in the register — one record per asset: cost, date, class, useful life, location, and cost center, so depreciation lands on the branch that uses the asset. Register rules:

1. Created at purchase — the purchase invoice's capitalisation flow feeds the register; the asset is born from its document, not reconstructed from a year-end spreadsheet.
2. Amended as governed events.
3. Retired by the disposal flow — never deleted.

Depreciation. Computed per asset from its class's method and life — straight-line is the trading business's standard — and posted monthly by the automated entry: DR depreciation expense (addressed by the asset's cost center), CR accumulated depreciation. The balance sheet carries cost less accumulated depreciation as net book value.

Disposals. When an asset is sold, scrapped, or traded in, the disposal flow closes its record: proceeds against net book value, the gain or loss posted, the register entry marked disposed with its date and evidence. An asset that physically left without a disposal entry leaves the register asserting property the business no longer holds.

The annual verification. The register is physically verified once a year — the fixed-asset equivalent of the stock count: each registered asset sighted (or its absence investigated and resolved through the disposal flow), locations and cost centers corrected, and the verification signed and filed. The balance sheet's fixed-asset line is only as reliable as the last verification.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Year-end, the audit, and the HealthTrade case
lessons.html:
Year-end is the twelfth monthly close plus a short list of annual mechanics. This chapter covers the mechanics, the external audit, and HealthTrade's close year.

The year-end additions.

1. The closing entries. The fiscal year's P&L accounts are closed to retained earnings by the period-closing voucher — one governed entry making the year's result equity's newest layer. This is the only routine way retained earnings ever moves.
2. Fiscal year mechanics. The new year opened in the system before its first document needs it; the closing performed on the accountant's calendar. The fiscal year need not be the calendar year; the system serves either.
3. The annual layer of every calendar — the full stock count, the asset verification, the chart and settings walks, module 5's annual returns — scheduled across the season, not stacked into one week.
4. The audit file. For a monthly-closing business, the file is the year's twelve close bundles plus the annual artifacts — assembled by collation, not creation.

The external audit. Its shape against a business that runs this track:

• The interim walk-through — the auditor tests the system of control: the tie, the bridges, the reconciliations, the separations. A business that passes walk-through earns sampling instead of full substantive testing, which is the audit-fee conversation in one sentence.
• Fieldwork — samples drilled to documents.
• Confirmations — module 4's circularisation, pre-answered by the year's hygiene.
• Adjustments — the auditor proposes some; the accountant agrees or contests them professionally; agreed adjustments are booked by module 2's rules — referenced entries in the current or formally reopened period, never quiet edits — so the audited statements and the ledger end the season as the same document.

HealthTrade's close year. The first close takes four days of backlog work: the document sweep finds eleven stragglers, suspense empties (₦93,000 across six items), and the first full checklist runs to signature. Month two closes in two days; by month five the close lands on day three and the statements are read on day five's standing meeting. The readings produce decisions within the quarter: the cash flow read exposes the growth squeeze (positive profit, negative operating cash from stock build), which triggers the purchasing ladder review; the P&L trend read catches a two-point margin slide decomposed to one branch's discounting; and the balance sheet walk retires the last unexplained line. At year-end, the audit's walk-through passes on first presentation, fieldwork samples rather than excavates, and the auditor's adjustments — three, all agreed — book by the rules. The audit closes three weeks earlier than the prior year, at a lower fee, with the statements and the ledger identical.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the seventh law
lessons.html:
The close-and-statements layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the never-closed month. Symptom: periods open for a year; statement dates nobody trusts; every report a draft. Cause: the close never instituted (Chapters 1-2). Fix: the first close performed once, honestly, with its backlog; then the checklist with named owners, the day-five target, and the freeze keeping each sealed month sealed.

Pattern 2 — the year-end backlog. Symptom: twelve months of accruals, reconciliations, and corrections processed in January; statements about a year nobody remembers. Cause: closing annually what should close monthly (Chapter 1) — every error twelve months stale by discovery. Fix: the monthly rhythm, which removes this pattern by construction.

Pattern 3 — the bouncing margin. Symptom: gross margin swinging month to month on stable trade; owners distrusting the P&L. Cause: cut-off noise read as news (Chapter 3) — the completeness pairs breaking at every boundary. Fix: the day-one document sweep, the To-Bill queues read in naira at every close, the RNB age watched, and Chapter 3's worked example taught to whoever reads the statements.

Pattern 4 — statements produced but not read. Symptom: the pages circulated and filed with no decision ever traced to them; the owner learning the business's position from the bank app. Cause: the reading habit never installed (Chapters 4-6). Fix: the twenty-minute monthly reading as a standing meeting, the reading methods of Chapters 4-6, and the three-number headline discipline.

Pattern 5 — the unexplained equity movement. Symptom: retained earnings shifting between periods with no closing entry behind it; equity used as a plug for whatever would not balance. Cause: the most serious failure here — history edited at its last hiding place (Chapters 5, 8). Deleted documents, forced balances, and migration errors all surface in equity. Fix: each movement traced to its cause (the GL always records it), the closing entry restored as retained earnings' only routine mover, deletion rights removed, and the equity line added to every monthly balance-sheet walk.

The review list. Confirm you can state: the close's definition and the case for monthly closing with the day-five target; the nine checklist lines in order and why the order matters; the three completeness pairs, the day-one sweep, and the ₦500,000 worked example; the P&L structure, the four reading rules, and the pre-reading checks; the balance-sheet line checks and the equity rule; the three cash flow sections and the four-question read; the capitalisation policy, the register rules, and the annual verification; and the year-end's four additions with the audit's shape.

The seventh law: the books close monthly, the statements are read monthly, and a sealed month stays sealed. Module 8 covers the settings, authorities, and calendar that hold the whole finance layer together.

advanced_accounts.title: Accounts 8 — Advanced Accounts: Settings, Controls & Structure
advanced_accounts.desc: The structural layer: the Accounts Settings walk, fiscal years and the companies-follow-legal-reality rule with inter-company disciplines, the four finance authorities and the permission matrix, the consolidated finance calendar, the handover and absence tests, the assembled control system with the pairing principle and the CSA, and the professional boundaries between the system role, the accountant, the tax adviser, and the auditor — closing with the track's eight laws.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Accounts Settings
lessons.html:
This final module covers the structural layer that holds the finance function together: the settings, the fiscal-year and multi-company mechanics, the separation of authorities, the consolidated calendar, the handover test, the assembled control system, and the professional boundaries. It opens with the settings walk — each field a policy the system will enforce silently on every transaction.

The settings walk, field by field. Performed with the accountant and the owner present; answers recorded in the implementation file; re-walked annually.

• Frozen entries and the frozen-edit role — the period lock's configuration (module 7's freeze). The frozen date's advance is part of the monthly close; the edit role is granted to two named people at most. Two health checks: a frozen date that never advances means the lock is not being used; a broadly granted edit role means the lock has no force.
• Credit control settings — the credit-limit machinery's master switches: who may override, and whether blocked documents hold or warn. The gate numbers' configured home.
• Payment and allocation settings — the automatic-allocation behaviours and the unlink-on-cancel setting: whether cancelling a payment silently unlinks its allocations. The wrong value here manufactures module 4's unallocated backlog on its own. For businesses trading in more than naira: the exchange gain/loss accounts wired and revaluation governed — the accountant's policy, the system's designated accounts.
• Deferred accounting automation — where the system spreads deferred revenue and expense by schedule (module 2's matching, automated): enabled deliberately, its accounts wired, its schedules reviewed like any template.
• Precision, rounding, and the round-off account — currency precision consistent everywhere (a mismatch between documents and ledgers produces kobo-level reconciliation noise permanently), and the round-off account pointed at its designated home.
• Naming series — invoices, payments, journals: chosen once with a long horizon, because the document numbers on a filed VAT return must still make sense to an auditor in year seven. Series are never restarted or reused.

The walk's rules.

1. Each field is read as the policy question it is, and the answer is written down.
2. Changes after go-live are governed events with a reason and a record — not toggles flipped per complaint.
3. The annual re-walk is a standing calendar line (Chapter 4), and it is the only routine occasion on which settings change.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Fiscal years and multiple companies
lessons.html:
Two structural mechanics of the finance layer: financial time is partitioned into fiscal years, and one system can hold several legal companies.

Fiscal years.

• Created ahead. The new fiscal year must exist before its first document needs it. The January 1st invoice that cannot post because nobody created the year is the most avoidable start-of-year failure; the standing practice is creating the next year at least two months early.
• Aligned to the statutory year. The calendar year for most Nigerian companies, but the system serves any twelve months; the accountant confirms.
• Closed in sequence. Module 7's closing entry per year, by the period-closing voucher.
• The year is also the container for budgets (module 6) and the axis for comparative reports — trend reads depend on clean year boundaries.
• Backdating across a closed fiscal year is the correction rules' most serious case: an entry into a closed year changes audited, filed figures. The default answer is module 2's rule — correct in the current period with remarks naming the original date. Formal reopening is the accountant's documented decision, and rare.

Multiple companies. The system's multi-company machinery gives each company its own chart (or a shared template with per-company accounts), its own fiscal calendar, and its own separately sealed books, inside one system where group-level users can see across.

The rule for when a second company is right: companies follow legal reality, never reporting convenience.

• Separate registered entities keep separate books because the law treats them as separate persons — the audit, the tax filings, and the liability wall all run per entity.
• A branch is a dimension (module 6). A branch promoted to a company because someone wanted "separate books" acquires statutory filing obligations to solve a reporting problem a dimension solves at no cost.

Inter-company transactions. Where entities genuinely transact — management fees, shared costs recharged, stock transferred, loans between entities — three rules apply:

1. Every inter-company transaction is documented in both entities: an invoice in one is a bill in the other, with mirrored references.
2. The inter-company balances are reconciled on a rhythm (Chapter 4 puts it quarterly): entity A's receivable from B equals B's payable to A, to the kobo.
3. Pricing and tax treatment of inter-company charges are the accountant's and tax adviser's territory — set as policy before the first charge, not improvised per invoice.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The four finance authorities
lessons.html:
The finance layer has four distinct authorities, and the control design consists of keeping them separated.

The four authorities.

1. Record — creating the documents and journals that write the ledger. Trading documents broadly; the journal pen narrowly (module 2's two names).
2. Release — moving actual money: the payment run's authoriser, the bank mandate's signatories (module 3's preparer-never-releaser rule).
3. Close — sealing and unsealing time: the freeze advance, the frozen-edit role, the fiscal year's closing (module 7 and Chapter 1).
4. Configure — the settings, the chart, the dimensions, the templates. The narrowest authority of all.

The design rule: the authorities check each other only if they are held by different people. The recorder's entries are paid by someone else's release; the releaser's payments are checked by someone else's reconciliation; the closer's seal is read by someone else's review; and nobody's routine role includes changing the configuration.

The pairings that must not collapse. The specific separations an audit tests first:

• The journal pen and the payment release in different hands. A person who can write any entry and also move any money holds, in one seat, the full opportunity for fraud.
• Payment preparer and releaser split — two people, at any size (module 3).
• The reconciler is not the sole releaser — the mover of money is not its only checker.
• Adjustment powers held narrow — the write-off's two names (module 4); the journal pen's two names (module 2).
• The frozen-edit role disjoint from the daily recorders — the person posting today should not be able to repost yesterday's sealed figures.

Sizing. At eleven people, roles share heads: the founder releases what the accountant prepares; the accountant closes what the founder's review checks. The irreducible pairs survive any size because each is two people, not two departments. A business too small for two people in finance is a business where the owner is one of the two — which is the standard SME arrangement, and a sound one.

The permission matrix. The four authorities, mapped to named people, documented on one page, reviewed annually and at every personnel change — the same treatment module 3 gave the bank mandate. The review's first question is always the same: does any one person hold more than one authority without a documented reason?

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The finance calendar
lessons.html:
The finance function runs on a consolidated calendar. This chapter states it once, by frequency. Each line has a named owner; the calendar itself lives on the policy page and is reviewed annually.

Daily.

• The cash position read: balances, reconciliation recency, the day's obligations (module 3).
• The exceptions scan: blocked documents, failed payments, till-session variances flagged overnight.
• Entry hygiene at the desks: references captured, dimensions cascading — the habits that keep every later routine cheap.

Weekly.

• The bank items sweep: new statement lines, charges booked from the statement, deposits matched.
• The unallocated glance: module 4's read at light cadence — items caught young allocate in minutes.
• The payment run cycle, where the business runs one: prepared, evidenced, released by separated hands.

Monthly — the anchor.

• The close checklist (module 7's nine lines), days one to five, containing as collected inputs: the AR/AP ritual (module 4's ninety minutes), the tax cycles (module 5's six steps per custody, zeroes verified), the journal review (module 2), the bank reconciliations (module 3, every account), and the dimension lump sweep (module 6).
• The statements reading with management (module 7's twenty minutes) — the calendar's most important meeting.
• The branch P&Ls issued and the budget variance read (module 6).

Quarterly.

• The provision review in depth — the matrix's judgments revisited (module 4).
• The correction log read by cause — upstream problems surfaced (module 2).
• The bank charges reasonableness read (module 3).
• The allocation pool audit — direct-first shrinking it (module 6).
• The advance agings' escalations resolved (module 4).
• Inter-company reconciliations, where they exist (Chapter 2).

Annually. Scheduled across weeks, not stacked:

• The settings walk (Chapter 1) and the permission matrix review (Chapter 3).
• The chart walk — every account explainable in one sentence (module 1).
• The dimension audit (module 6) and the bank mandate review (module 3).
• The capitalisation policy review and the asset verification (module 7).
• The budget build (module 6 — November).
• The compliance calendar re-confirmed against current law (module 5).
• The year-end mechanics (module 7).

Practical rule: a calendar line without a named owner is a line that will stop running. The annual review's first task is confirming every line still has one.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The finance handover test
lessons.html:
The handover test asks one question of any function: could a competent newcomer, given only what is documented, run it for a month with zero questions that only the departing person can answer? Finance — the function most often held entirely in one trusted accountant's head — needs the test most.

The test, walked module by module. A finance function passes when:

1. The chart documents the account language, every account with its one-sentence purpose (module 1).
2. The journal governance is written: the pen's two names, the recurring template set, the correction rules (module 2).
3. The bank layer is documented: every account, mode, and mandate, with last month's reconciliations showing where each remainder stands (module 3).
4. The AR/AP ritual's checklist and policy pages state the tie, the matrix, and the write-off path (module 4).
5. The compliance calendar lists every obligation, day, authority, and evidence folder — with twelve months of folders showing the pattern (module 5).
6. The dimension design is documented and the allocation policy answers every sharing question by pointing (module 6).
7. The close checklist states the month's spine in nine ordered lines, and the statement-reading method is written (module 7).
8. This module's calendar, permission matrix, and settings record hold the structure.

Every "no" in the walk identifies a module incompletely done. The documentation is not an extra deliverable — it is the by-product of each module done properly.

The absence test. The practical version: the key person takes uninterrupted leave, and the function runs on its calendar. What breaks during the absence is exactly what the documentation is missing. Run deliberately, the absence test is the cheapest audit of function structure available, and its findings are corrected without crisis.

The role path. A documented function also makes progression legible: the bookkeeper (entries and desk hygiene) grows into the accountant (the close's owner, the journal pen's holder, the statements' first reader), who grows into the controller (the calendar's owner, the policies' custodian, the management reading's co-chair). Clean closes, young remainders, and tied bridges form a promotion case written in numbers. The alternative — the function running entirely in one trusted head — is a single point of failure regardless of how competent the head is, and Chapter 9's Pattern 5 treats it as such.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Internal controls, assembled
lessons.html:
The track installed controls one module at a time. Assembled, they form a system with two families, and this chapter is the map.

The two families.

• Preventive controls stop an error or fraud before it posts: the separations (the four authorities, the two-names patterns), the validations (mandatory parties, mandatory dimensions, the balance rule), the fences (the forbidden journal list, frozen periods, masters-not-messages), and the gates (approval thresholds, the release separation).
• Detective controls catch what slipped through: the reconciliations (bank, supplier-statement), the ties (controls-to-parties, the bridges, the zeroing invariant), the reviews (the journal review, the trial-balance scan, the adjustments read), and the aged reads (remainder agings, the correction log, the unallocated list).

The pairing principle. Every preventive control should have a detective partner watching its gaps: journal governance prevents, the journal review detects; the release separation prevents, the reconciliation detects; mandatory dimensions prevent, the lump sweep detects. A control map with unpaired fences has blind spots — the assembly check is walking the map and naming each control's partner.

The fraud triangle. The standard frame: fraud requires opportunity (access plus an absent control), pressure (personal circumstances nobody sees), and rationalisation (the story the person tells themselves). The business controls only opportunity — which is what the preventive family shrinks: the everything-role dismantled, custody segregated, the journal pen narrowed, the masters guarded. The detective family then shortens the time to discovery: what would compound for years surfaces at the month's reconciliation. The cultural layer removes rationalisation's easiest story: controls framed as protecting the honest holder — the clean count, the signed run, the documented approval are the honest person's own evidence — are harder to resent and harder to excuse breaking.

The control self-assessment (CSA). Annual, on evidence, one page per control: does it still run, and can it prove it ran?

1. List the controls by family.
2. For each, name the evidence of its last execution (the reconciliation file, the review sign-off, the approval log).
3. Read the tell-tale metrics: approval times (a second signature granted in seconds is not a review), remainder ages, sweep sizes.
4. Revive or formally retire dead controls. A designed-but-dead control is worse than an absent one, because someone is relying on it.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Professional boundaries: accountant, tax adviser, auditor
lessons.html:
The finance layer is run with three professionals, and the boundaries between the system role and each of them must be held clearly. This chapter states the boundary map and the working patterns.

The boundary map.

• The system role — the person who configures and operates the machinery (this certification's territory) — owns the configuration, the templates, the registers, the routines, the evidence structure, and the literacy to walk any entry with any professional. It does not make policy judgments.
• The accountant owns the policy: method choices, provision matrices, capitalisation thresholds, recognition schedules, reopening decisions, and professional responsibility for the statements.
• The tax adviser owns the positions: rates, eligibility, reliefs, and stances where the law is unclear (module 5's boundary).
• The auditor owns the opinion: independent, sample-based, and best served by being served organised evidence (module 7's file).

The dividing sentence, worth memorising because it will be blurred monthly: the machinery makes the professionals' judgments executable and evidenced; it does not make the judgments.

The working patterns.

1. The accountant co-designs from day one. The chart walk, the posting-map verification, and the policy pages are done with the accountant in the room. An accounts layer built without the accountant who must own it gets built twice.
2. Habit conflicts resolve by evidence, not authority. Where the system's discipline conflicts with an accountant's established habit — module 2's journal-habit case is the standard example — the resolution is demonstration and transfer, not derision.
3. The auditor is engaged early. The interim walk-through invited rather than endured, the file structure shared in advance, adjustments booked by the correction rules. The audit relationship compounds across years the same way the authority relationship does: a clean first year buys a lighter second.
4. The tax adviser is consulted before configuration, not after. The new revenue stream's VAT treatment, related-party pricing, and reform eligibility questions are settled before the templates are built — reconfiguring after a wrong position costs far more than the consultation.

Summary. Machinery, policy, positions, opinion — four owners. Hold the boundary, co-design with the accountant, meet the auditor early, and loop the tax adviser in before configuring anything the law touches.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's structural year
lessons.html:
The structural layer, installed over four quarters. Each chapter of this module appears.

Q1 — the settings walk (Chapters 1-2). The walk runs with the accountant. Frozen entries are configured with the two-name edit role and the freeze advance is added to the close checklist. The unlink-on-cancel setting is found at its wrong value — it had been silently unlinking allocations whenever a payment was cancelled, which explained part of module 4's original unallocated backlog — and corrected. Naming series are confirmed for the long term. The next fiscal year is created two months early, closing off the January 1st failure before it can occur. Every answer is recorded in the implementation file.

Q2 — the permission matrix (Chapter 3). The review finds the implementation-era all-permissions role still live on one user: the accountant, holding record, release, close, and configure "temporarily" since go-live. It is dismantled as a design exercise, not an accusation: the journal pen and the payment release are split (the founder releases what the accountant prepares — the two roles the business's size allows, correctly separated), the frozen-edit role is confirmed at two names, and the matrix is documented on one page. At the next audit, the walk-through passes its separation tests for the first time.

Q3 — the control self-assessment (Chapter 6). The first CSA walks the control map by family and finds one designed-but-dead control: the second signature on large journals, live in the workflow but rubber-stamped in practice — approvals landing in seconds, unread. It is revived with an evidence habit: the approver samples the journal's references before signing, and approval times are read quarterly. The CSA also confirms the pairing principle across the map — every fence has its detective partner — and files its one-page-per-control record.

Q4 — the absence test (Chapter 5). The founder takes three uninterrupted weeks. The trading functions had passed the test in earlier years; this year finance runs on its calendar: the close lands on day five without the founder's review, the payment runs release under the deputy-mandate design, and the compliance calendar's two in-window filings land on their days. The handover walk afterwards scores its first clean sheet — zero founder-only questions in the finance function. The MD's note in the year file: the business now runs on its documents in every function, including the one that counts them.

The year in numbers. Close: day five, every month of H2. Audit: walk-through passed, three agreed adjustments, fee reduced. Unallocated read: near-zero every month since the unlink fix. Permission matrix: four authorities, no undocumented overlaps. Absence test: passed.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes, the eighth law & the track's laws
lessons.html:
The structural layer's recurring failures, the module's law, and the track's eight laws assembled.

Pattern 1 — settings changed casually. Symptom: frozen dates that never advance; the unlink setting flipped per complaint; precision changed mid-year. Cause: the settings treated as toggles instead of policy (Chapter 1). Fix: settings behind the narrowest authority, changes as governed events with a record, and the annual walk as the only routine occasion for change.

Pattern 2 — the everything-role. Symptom: one user holding record, release, close, and configure; the audit walk-through's first finding. Cause: setup convenience never dismantled (Chapter 3) — the full fraud opportunity assembled in one seat. Fix: the four authorities separated by the two-people patterns, the matrix documented and reviewed annually, and the dismantling run as a design exercise, not an accusation.

Pattern 3 — the branch promoted to a company. Symptom: statutory filings multiplying; inter-company balances nobody reconciles; "separate books" that a dimension would have provided at no cost. Cause: companies created for reporting convenience instead of legal reality (Chapter 2). Fix: dimensions for reading, companies for legal persons, and the wrongly created entity wound down or made legally real with the accountant.

Pattern 4 — designed-but-dead controls. Symptom: reconciliations that quietly stopped; second signatures granted in seconds; checklist lines dropped. Cause: false assurance (Chapter 6) — worse than absence, because someone relies on the control. Fix: the annual CSA on evidence, the approval-time and remainder-age metrics, and dead controls revived or formally retired.

Pattern 5 — the single-person function. Symptom: finance running entirely in one trusted head; leave never taken; a close only one person can perform; an owner who cannot read the statements unaided. Cause: competence without structure (Chapter 5) — a single point of failure regardless of skill. Fix: the handover test as the standard, the documentation as each module's by-product, the role path making structure a promotion engine, and the absence test run deliberately.

The review list. Confirm you can state: the settings walk's fields and the three walk rules; the fiscal-year rules and the companies-follow-legal-reality rule with the three inter-company disciplines; the four authorities, the pairings that must not collapse, and the sizing answer; the calendar by frequency; the handover test's eight-point walk and the absence test; the two control families, the pairing principle, the fraud triangle, and the CSA; and the four professional boundaries with the four working patterns.

The eighth law: structure over individuals — authorities separated, settings governed, rhythms on the calendar, and the function passes the handover test.

The track's eight laws.

1. The books are written by documents, into a chart designed for reading.
2. The journal is the exception and the document is the rule — what a document can do, a document must do.
3. Every bank account is reconciled monthly, and every difference is named — never plugged.
4. The chair keeps the record real, collectable, current and complete.
5. Tax money is held, not owned — reconciled, filed from the system, remitted from the reserve, and zeroed every cycle.
6. One chart, many lenses — every posting carries its address, contribution decides, and allocation is written.
7. The books close monthly, the statements are read monthly, and a sealed month stays sealed.
8. Structure over individuals — authorities separated, settings governed, rhythms on the calendar, and the function passes the handover test.

This completes the Accounts Professional track.
